meta.blurb: Dorothy's farmhouse lands on a witch, and the dead witch's silver shoes end up on Dorothy's feet. Now she must follow the yellow road to a Wizard who might send her home. His price is another witch's life.
meta.bible: Dorothy: a kind, brave little girl from a Kansas farm. Toto: her small black dog. Aunt Em: Dorothy's aunt, gray and tired. Uncle Henry: Dorothy's uncle, a quiet farmer. Kansas: the flat, gray prairie where Dorothy lives. Cyclone: the storm that lifts the house. Oz: the Land of Oz, a magic country with four parts. Munchkins: the small blue people of the East. Winkies: the yellow people of the West. Quadlings: the red people of the South. Wicked Witch of the East: crushed by the house. Wicked Witch of the West: has one eye like a telescope, fears water. Good Witch of the North: a kind old woman who guides Dorothy. Glinda: the Good Witch of the South, young and beautiful. Silver Shoes: magic shoes from the Witch of the East. Yellow Brick Road: the road to the Emerald City. Emerald City: the green city where the Wizard lives. Scarecrow: made of straw, wants brains, is really wise. Tin Woodman: made of tin, wants a heart, is really kind. Cowardly Lion: wants courage, is really brave. Wizard: the Great Oz, really a kind old man from Omaha and a humbug. Omaha: the Wizard's home city in America. Boq: a Munchkin who feeds Dorothy. Kalidahs: fierce beasts with the heads of tigers and the bodies of bears. Poppies: red flowers whose smell makes you sleep. Field Mice: small helpers led by their Queen. Stork: the bird who saves Scarecrow. Winged Monkeys: flying servants of the Golden Cap, led by their King. Golden Cap: a magic cap that gives three wishes. Fighting Trees: trees that grab travelers. China Country: a land of living china people. Hammer-Heads: rude people with heads like hammers. Balloon: the Wizard's way of leaving. Cellar: the hole under the floor where the family hides from storms. Soldier with the Green Whiskers: the palace guard who opens the Wizard's doors. Guardian of the Gates: the small man who locks green spectacles on every visitor. Spectacles: green glasses that make the Emerald City look green. Monkey King: leader of the Winged Monkeys; his grandfather played a trick on Quelala. Quelala: the young man Gayelette loved; Gayelette: a princess and sorceress of the North who made the Golden Cap. Tinsmith: the Winkie metal workers who mend the Tin Woodman. Humbug: the Wizard's own word for himself. Ventriloquist: someone who throws the voice. Queen of the Field Mice: the small queen the Tin Woodman saves from a wildcat. Hill of the Hammer-Heads: the steep hill near the forest of the beasts. Spider: the huge monster of the forest, killed by the Lion. Glinda's ruby throne and red castle stand in the country of the Quadlings. Dorothy's gingham dress is blue and white; the Silver Shoes are lost in the desert at the end. Wolves, Crows, Bees: the Witch's three attacks. Quadling country: red houses, red fields and plump, kind people. Voice and tone: warm, simple, bright and a little funny; danger is real but never gory; the ending is gentle and joyful.

beats.scene: Dorothy and Toto stand before a small gray house on a flat gray prairie
beats.summary: Dorothy lives with her dog Toto on a flat, gray Kansas prairie.

beats.scene: A small plain house with one room, a stove, a cupboard and two beds
beats.summary: The farmhouse is tiny, with one room and no cellar except a hole under the floor.

beats.scene: Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, both gray and tired, stand beside Dorothy and Toto
beats.summary: Years of sun and wind have turned Aunt Em and Uncle Henry gray, and only Toto makes Dorothy laugh.

beats.scene: Uncle Henry sits at the door and stares at the dark sky
beats.summary: One afternoon Uncle Henry sees the sky darken and hears the wind coming.

beats.scene: The tall grass bends in long waves while Uncle Henry runs toward the barn
beats.summary: Uncle Henry sees the grass bend and runs to the animals, shouting about a cyclone.

beats.scene: Aunt Em lifts the trap door in the floor and points down the ladder
beats.summary: Aunt Em opens the trap door and tells Dorothy to run for the cellar.

beats.scene: Toto hides under a big bed while Dorothy reaches for him
beats.summary: Dorothy catches Toto, but the house shakes and she falls before she reaches the cellar.

beats.scene: The little farmhouse spins in the air high above the gray prairie
beats.summary: The house whirls around twice and rises slowly into the air like a balloon.

beats.scene: Dorothy lies on her bed while the dark house floats through the sky
beats.summary: Dorothy lies on her bed with Toto and soon falls asleep as the house floats on.

beats.scene: Sunshine floods a quiet green meadow around a house that has just landed
beats.summary: A sudden shock wakes Dorothy, and she finds the house resting in bright sunshine.

beats.scene: Dorothy stands in a doorway looking out at a green meadow full of flowers
beats.summary: Dorothy opens the door and sees a beautiful green country.

beats.scene: Fruit trees, bright flowers, singing birds and a brook fill a green meadow
beats.summary: She sees fruit trees, bright flowers, singing birds and a sparkling brook.

beats.scene: Three small men in blue and an old woman walk toward the house
beats.summary: Three small men and an old woman come toward the house.

beats.scene: A tiny old woman in a starry white gown bows to Dorothy
beats.summary: The old woman greets Dorothy and thanks her for killing the Wicked Witch of the East.

beats.scene: Dorothy looks puzzled and holds Toto while the old woman smiles
beats.summary: Dorothy says there is a mistake, because she has not killed anyone.

beats.scene: Two feet in silver shoes stick out from under a corner of the house
beats.summary: The old woman points to two feet in silver shoes sticking out from under the house.

beats.scene: Munchkins in blue gather to explain how they were slaves to a witch
beats.summary: The Munchkins explain that the Witch of the East kept them as slaves for many years.

beats.scene: Dorothy weeps beside the old woman, who looks kindly at her
beats.summary: Dorothy longs to go home, but the old woman says no road leads out of Oz.

beats.scene: The old woman kisses Dorothy's forehead beside a road of yellow bricks
beats.summary: The Witch advises her to seek the Wizard in the Emerald City, and kisses her for protection.

beats.scene: Dorothy puts the silver shoes on her feet while the Witch spins away
beats.summary: Dorothy takes the silver shoes and packs bread, and the Witch of the North spins away and vanishes.

beats.scene: Dorothy ties on a clean apron while Toto waits beside a basket
beats.summary: Dorothy washes, puts on her clean dress, packs her basket and sets out with Toto.

beats.scene: A yellow brick road stretches between blue fences and green fields
beats.summary: She finds the yellow brick road and walks along it, with Munchkin farms on every side.

beats.scene: Blue-roofed Munchkin houses and neat blue fences line the road
beats.summary: Munchkin houses and blue fences line the road, and the farmers wave and bow.

beats.scene: Dorothy and Toto stand before a large blue house where Munchkins dance
beats.summary: Toward evening Dorothy comes to a large house where many Munchkins are dancing.

beats.scene: A smiling rich Munchkin named Boq welcomes Dorothy at his front door
beats.summary: Boq, a rich Munchkin, welcomes Dorothy because she has killed the witch.

beats.scene: Dorothy eats a big supper at a long table while Toto eats his bones
beats.summary: Dorothy eats a big supper at the long table while the Munchkins watch.

beats.scene: Boq and Dorothy talk by lamplight while the guests listen
beats.summary: Boq asks where she is going and warns that the Great Oz is hard to find and see.

beats.scene: Dorothy sleeps in a soft white bed while Toto lies on a blue rug
beats.summary: Dorothy sleeps in a comfortable bed while Toto lies on a blue rug.

beats.scene: Dorothy and Toto walk away from Boq's blue house in morning light
beats.summary: In the morning Dorothy eats breakfast, thanks Boq and walks on.

beats.scene: A scarecrow on a long pole in a green cornfield stares at Dorothy
beats.summary: Dorothy comes to a cornfield where a scarecrow on a pole seems to look at her.

beats.scene: The painted scarecrow winks one eye at astonished Dorothy
beats.summary: The scarecrow winks, nods and greets Dorothy, and says he is tired of hanging there.

beats.scene: Dorothy lifts the Scarecrow from his pole in the middle of a cornfield
beats.summary: Dorothy lifts the Scarecrow off the pole, and he is very light.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow shakes out his arms and legs as straw drifts down
beats.summary: He shakes himself, pats his straw back into shape, and feels like a new man.

beats.scene: Dorothy points down the yellow road while the Scarecrow scratches his painted head
beats.summary: Dorothy tells him her name and that she is going to the Emerald City to ask the Wizard for help.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow sadly pokes his straw head while crows sit on the fence
beats.summary: He explains that he has no brains, because he is stuffed with straw, and tells how a crow taught him this.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow bends toward Dorothy with a hopeful look on his painted face
beats.summary: The Scarecrow asks to go with Dorothy and ask the Wizard for brains, and she is glad.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow stumbles over a missing brick while Toto sniffs the hole
beats.summary: The Scarecrow stumbles on a hole in the road, laughs and gets up unhurt.

beats.scene: Dorothy and the Scarecrow talk as they walk across a bright green countryside
beats.summary: The Scarecrow says he cannot understand why she wants to leave this beautiful land for gray Kansas.

beats.scene: A small house beside the road glows in the evening while Dorothy eats bread
beats.summary: At night they reach a small house, where Dorothy eats bread and sleeps while the Scarecrow stands in a corner.

beats.scene: Dorothy fills a bucket at a brook while the road enters a dark forest
beats.summary: In the morning they walk on until the road enters a dense forest, and they hear a groan.

beats.scene: A low groan drifts through dark trees as Dorothy and the Scarecrow stop
beats.summary: Deep in the forest the travelers hear a low groan.

beats.scene: A tin man stands frozen with a raised axe beside a half-cut tree
beats.summary: They find a man made of tin, standing as still as a statue with his axe raised.

beats.scene: The tin man's eyes turn slowly toward Dorothy, though his jaws will not move
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman can only move his eyes, and he groans to ask for oil.

beats.scene: Dorothy runs to a small tin cottage and comes out with an oil can
beats.summary: Dorothy runs to the Woodman's cottage and brings back an oil can.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow gently bends the Tin Woodman's neck while Dorothy oils his elbow
beats.summary: The oil frees his neck, jaws and elbows, and the Tin Woodman can move again.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman bows to his rescuers and wipes away a tear
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman thanks them warmly, for he would have stood there forever.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman sits on a log with his hand on his chest
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman says he wants a heart and begins his story.

beats.scene: A young woodman in the forest swings his axe near a small cottage
beats.summary: He was once a woodman who cared for his old mother and fell in love with a Munchkin girl.

beats.scene: A witch waves her stick over a woodman's axe while an old woman watches
beats.summary: The girl's old guardian does not want to lose her, so she asks the Witch of the East to stop the wedding.

beats.scene: A tinsmith fits a shining tin leg onto the woodman beside a forge
beats.summary: The axe cuts off his leg, and a tinsmith makes him a new one out of tin.

beats.scene: The tinsmith hammers new tin arms and a tin head for the woodman
beats.summary: The enchanted axe cuts off his other leg, both arms and his head, and each time the tinsmith makes tin ones.

beats.scene: The tinsmith bends over a shining tin body in his workshop
beats.summary: At last the axe cuts his body in two, and the tinsmith gives him a tin body, but he has no heart.

beats.scene: The tin man stands in heavy rain while his joints turn orange with rust
beats.summary: Rain rusts him still, and he stands for a year, wishing for a heart.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman, the Scarecrow and Dorothy discuss brains and hearts under tall trees
beats.summary: He asks to join them to ask Oz for a heart, and the Scarecrow thinks brains are better.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman takes his axe and his oil can while Dorothy smiles
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman joins them, carrying his axe and his oil can.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman kneels sadly over a small beetle on the yellow road
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman steps on a beetle by accident and cries, so that his jaws rust.

beats.scene: Dorothy and her friends sit by a small campfire in a dark forest
beats.summary: At night they camp under a tree, where the Scarecrow gathers nuts for Dorothy.

beats.scene: A huge lion leaps from the dark trees, roaring with open jaws
beats.summary: A great Lion springs out of the forest with a roar and knocks the Scarecrow over.

beats.scene: The Lion strikes the Tin Woodman, who stands firm, and Toto barks fiercely
beats.summary: The Lion strikes the Tin Woodman, but he only dents his claws, and then goes after Toto.

beats.scene: Dorothy slaps the Lion on the nose while Toto tugs at his tail
beats.summary: Dorothy runs forward and slaps the Lion on the nose to save Toto.

beats.scene: The Lion rubs his nose while Dorothy shakes a finger at him
beats.summary: The Lion says he did not bite Toto, and Dorothy scolds him for trying, and for hitting a stuffed man.

beats.scene: The Lion wipes a tear with the tip of his tail beside the fire
beats.summary: The Lion confesses that he was born a coward, and that his roar frightens every animal away.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman and the Lion talk gently while the others listen
beats.summary: The Woodman says the Lion should be glad to have a heart, and the Lion wonders if he is better off without one.

beats.scene: The Lion and the three friends and a dog cross a wide ditch together
beats.summary: The Lion joins them to ask the Wizard for courage, and on the road he carries them over a wide ditch.

beats.scene: A dark forest where Dorothy and the Lion whisper about a strange beast
beats.summary: In a darker part of the forest they hear growls, and the Lion tells them about the fierce Kalidahs.

beats.scene: A deeper ditch crosses the road, with a tall tree growing at its edge
beats.summary: They reach another ditch, too wide for even the Lion, and the Scarecrow has an idea about a tree.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman chops a big tree and it falls across the ditch
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman cuts down the tree, and it falls across the ditch to make a bridge.

beats.scene: Two huge beasts with tiger heads chase after the friends on a log bridge
beats.summary: As they start to cross, two Kalidahs rush out of the forest, and the Lion roars in fear.

beats.scene: The two Kalidahs fall into the deep gap as the tree crashes down
beats.summary: The Lion crosses last, and the Tin Woodman chops the tree down, so that the Kalidahs fall into the ditch.

beats.scene: Dorothy and her friends build a raft of logs beside a broad river
beats.summary: Beyond the forest they come to a wide river, and the Tin Woodman builds a raft.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow clings to a pole as the raft sails away
beats.summary: The Scarecrow poles the raft, but the pole sticks in the mud and he is left hanging in midstream.

beats.scene: The Lion swims while the Tin Woodman holds his tail and pulls the raft
beats.summary: The Lion swims and tows the raft, with the Tin Woodman holding his tail, until they reach the shore.

beats.scene: A long-legged stork flies down and lifts the Scarecrow from his pole
beats.summary: A stork carries the Scarecrow to the bank, where his friends are glad to see him again.

beats.scene: Dorothy and the Lion stand at the edge of a red poppy field
beats.summary: The friends see a wide field of bright red poppies, and the sweet smell makes Dorothy sleepy.

beats.scene: Dorothy and Toto lie asleep among red poppies beside the sleeping Lion
beats.summary: Dorothy and the Lion fall asleep in the poppies, and Toto falls asleep too.

beats.scene: Two friends carry sleeping Dorothy and Toto out of the poppies
beats.summary: The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, who cannot sleep, carry Dorothy and Toto out of the poppies.

beats.scene: A wildcat chases a tiny field mouse past the Tin Woodman and Scarecrow
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman chases a wildcat away from a field mouse, and the mouse thanks him.

beats.scene: A small gray Queen of the field mice bows
beats.summary: The mouse is the Queen of all the Field Mice, and she offers to help them in return.

beats.scene: Hundreds of mice tied to strings pull a little wooden truck holding the Lion
beats.summary: Hundreds of mice come, and with the Tin Woodman's wooden truck they pull the sleeping Lion out of the poppies.

beats.scene: The Lion wakes and stretches beside a stream while mice scamper away
beats.summary: The Lion wakes, the mice leave, and the Queen promises to help again if they ever call.

beats.scene: Green fences and green houses line the yellow road under a green-tinted sky
beats.summary: The country grows greener as they walk, with green fences, houses and clothes.

beats.scene: Four friends sleep under trees while a green glow shines on the horizon
beats.summary: They sleep beside the road, and a green glow shines in the sky ahead.

beats.scene: A tall green wall with a gate of shining emeralds
beats.summary: In the morning they see the city's high green wall, and a gate studded with emeralds.

beats.scene: A small green man opens the gate and stares at the visitors
beats.summary: The Guardian of the Gates asks what they want and warns them that Oz is terrible to the dishonest.

beats.scene: The Guardian opens a huge box full of green glasses of every size
beats.summary: The Guardian says everyone must wear green spectacles, or the brightness of the city would blind them.

beats.scene: The Guardian locks green spectacles behind a lion's mane with a gold key
beats.summary: The Guardian fits spectacles on everyone, even Toto and the Lion, and locks them with a golden key.

beats.scene: Green marble houses and a tall green tower shine along a crowded street
beats.summary: They walk through streets of beautiful green houses, all shining with emeralds.

beats.scene: Green candy, green popcorn and green shoes fill the stalls of a bright market
beats.summary: Shops sell green candy, popcorn, shoes and clothes, and children play in green dresses.

beats.scene: A soldier with a long green beard stands at the palace door
beats.summary: At the palace the soldier with the green whiskers lets them in and tells them to wait.

beats.scene: A girl in green leads Dorothy to a green bedroom
beats.summary: A green maid shows Dorothy to a room, dresses her in green silk and ties a green ribbon on Toto.

beats.scene: Dorothy faces a giant head on a green throne
beats.summary: In the morning Dorothy is led to the throne room, where a huge head sits on a throne.

beats.scene: The giant head speaks to a frightened Dorothy and looks at her silver shoes
beats.summary: The head says he is Oz the Great and Terrible, and asks about her silver shoes and the mark on her forehead.

beats.scene: Dorothy cries in front of the great green head, which does not move
beats.summary: Oz says he will help Dorothy only if she kills the Wicked Witch of the West, and Dorothy cries.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow gazes at a beautiful lady with gauzy wings on the green throne
beats.summary: The next day the Scarecrow sees a beautiful lady with wings, and asks her for brains.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman faces a terrible beast with five eyes and woolly legs
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman faces a terrible beast and asks for a heart.

beats.scene: The Lion crouches before a huge ball of fire which burns on the throne
beats.summary: The Lion meets a ball of fire, asks for courage, and gets the same answer.

beats.scene: Dorothy sits in a green room with her friends, who all look sad
beats.summary: The friends meet in Dorothy's room, and each tells what he saw, and each saw something different.

beats.scene: The four friends stand in a circle and make a plan with serious faces
beats.summary: The friends decide to go together to find the Witch, although the Lion is afraid.

beats.scene: The Guardian unlocks the green spectacles at the city gate
beats.summary: In the morning the Guardian of the Gates unlocks their spectacles and tells them to go west.

beats.scene: Dorothy in a white dress walks across green meadows with her friends
beats.summary: They leave the city, and Dorothy sees that her dress and Toto's ribbon have turned white.

beats.scene: The one-eyed Witch watches from her yellow castle door
beats.summary: The Wicked Witch of the West has one eye as powerful as a telescope, and she sees them from far away.

beats.scene: A pack of great gray wolves races across a dark hillside toward the travelers
beats.summary: The Witch whistles for a pack of wolves and orders them to tear the travelers to pieces.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman swings his axe at charging wolves while the Scarecrow hides Dorothy
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman stands bravely with his axe and defeats forty wolves one by one.

beats.scene: A great black cloud of crows swoops down over the open grass
beats.summary: In the morning the Witch sees her dead wolves, grows angry and calls a flock of crows to peck out their eyes.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow waves his straw arms at a flock of black crows
beats.summary: The Scarecrow stands alone against the crows and twists the neck of each in turn.

beats.scene: A swarm of black bees buzzes in a dark cloud across the sky
beats.summary: The Witch next sends a swarm of black bees to sting them to death.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman stands shining among bees while straw covers Dorothy and the Lion
beats.summary: The Woodman tells the Scarecrow to cover Dorothy and the Lion with his straw, and the bees break their stingers on the Woodman.

beats.scene: Winkies in yellow run away from the Lion's loud roar
beats.summary: The Witch sends a band of Winkies with spears, but the Lion roars and they run away.

beats.scene: The Witch takes a golden cap with diamonds and rubies from a shelf
beats.summary: The Witch takes the Golden Cap from her cupboard, which lets her call the Winged Monkeys three times.

beats.scene: Winged Monkeys with gray wings and bright jackets fly to the Witch's call
beats.summary: The Witch speaks the magic words, the Winged Monkeys come, and she orders them to destroy all but the Lion.

beats.scene: Winged Monkeys drop the Tin Woodman on rocks and hurl straw into a tree
beats.summary: The Monkeys drop the Tin Woodman on sharp rocks and throw the Scarecrow's straw and clothes into a tall tree.

beats.scene: A lion bound in coils of rope is carried over the Witch's yellow land
beats.summary: The rest of the Monkeys tie the Lion with thick ropes and carry him to the Witch's castle.

beats.scene: A Monkey King kneels gently before Dorothy and points to her forehead
beats.summary: The Monkeys cannot harm Dorothy because of the Good Witch's kiss, and they carry her gently to the castle.

beats.scene: The Wicked Witch glares at Dorothy's silver shoes with a frightened face
beats.summary: The Witch sees the mark and the silver shoes and is afraid, but she sees that Dorothy does not know their power.

beats.scene: Dorothy scrubs pots and sweeps the floor in a big stone kitchen
beats.summary: The Witch takes Dorothy to the kitchen and makes her clean pots, sweep and feed the fire.

beats.scene: The Witch backs away from the roaring Lion in his iron yard
beats.summary: The Witch tries to harness the Lion, but he roars, so she starves him, and Dorothy brings him food at night.

beats.scene: Dorothy trips over an invisible iron bar in the kitchen
beats.summary: The Witch makes an iron bar invisible, so that Dorothy trips and one silver shoe falls off.

beats.scene: Dorothy flings a bucket of water over the angry Witch in the kitchen
beats.summary: Dorothy is so angry that she throws a bucket of water over the Witch.

beats.scene: The Witch melts into a brown puddle on the kitchen floor
beats.summary: The Witch begins to shrink and melt, and she cries that she did not think a girl could end her wickedness.

beats.scene: Dorothy sweeps the brown puddle out of the door and finds the silver shoe
beats.summary: Dorothy throws more water over what is left of the Witch, sweeps it out, and gets her silver shoe back.

beats.scene: Dorothy unlocks the iron gate while the Lion leaps out joyfully
beats.summary: Dorothy tells the Lion that the Witch is dead, and the Lion is free.

beats.scene: Yellow Winkies cheer in the castle yard as the Lion walks among them
beats.summary: The Winkies, who were slaves for many years, come out and thank them with great joy.

beats.scene: Winkies carry a dented tin man over a rocky field toward the castle
beats.summary: Dorothy asks the Winkies to help her find the Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow, and they find the Woodman on the rocks.

beats.scene: Winkie tinsmiths hammer the dented Tin Woodman at their workbench
beats.summary: Some of the Winkies are tinsmiths, and they straighten the Tin Woodman with hammers for three days and four nights.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman, polished and bright, raises his axe and smiles
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman is mended and polished, and he weeps for joy as he thanks Dorothy.

beats.scene: A tall tree holds a bundle of old clothes in its top branches
beats.summary: The Winkies lead them to the tall tree where the Scarecrow's clothes hang high above the ground.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman chops at a tall tree trunk while Winkies watch
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman chops the tree down, and the Winkies pick up the Scarecrow's clothes.

beats.scene: Winkies stuff the Scarecrow's clothes with fresh straw beside a happy Dorothy
beats.summary: The Winkies stuff the Scarecrow's clothes with clean straw, and he is happy to be himself again.

beats.scene: The Winkies kneel before the Tin Woodman and offer him a golden crown
beats.summary: The Winkies beg the Tin Woodman to rule over them, but he says that he must first go to the Wizard for his heart.

beats.scene: Dorothy puts on the shining Golden Cap she found in the Witch's cupboard
beats.summary: Dorothy finds the Golden Cap in the Witch's cupboard, puts it on, and the friends start back toward the Emerald City.

beats.scene: Four friends stand lost in a wide empty field with no road in sight
beats.summary: The friends walk east but lose their way, because there is no road in the Witch's old country.

beats.scene: Dorothy reads words inside the Golden Cap while her friends watch hopefully
beats.summary: Dorothy remembers the Golden Cap and says the magic words to call the Winged Monkeys.

beats.scene: The Monkey King bows to Dorothy while the other Monkeys wait in the sky
beats.summary: Dorothy asks the Monkeys to carry them to the Emerald City, and the King agrees, for the cap is hers now.

beats.scene: The Monkey King tells a tale about a prince who fell into a river
beats.summary: On the flight the Monkey King tells Dorothy why the Monkeys must obey the Cap.

beats.scene: Monkeys drop a young man in fine clothes into a river by a palace
beats.summary: His grandfather dropped Quelala, Gayelette's husband-to-be, into a river, and the princess punished the Monkeys.

beats.scene: The Monkeys set the friends down before the green city gate
beats.summary: The Monkeys set them down at the gate of the Emerald City, and the Guardian is amazed to see them.

beats.scene: Dorothy and the Lion wait in a green room
beats.summary: Oz will not see them, though they wait for days, and they grow very sad and angry.

beats.scene: Four friends and a trembling Lion enter the Throne Room
beats.summary: At last the soldier tells them that Oz will see them, and in the Throne Room a voice asks what they want.

beats.scene: Toto pulls a green screen aside, showing a little old man at a lever
beats.summary: Oz asks if the Witch is really dead and tells them to come back tomorrow, so the Lion roars, and Toto knocks over the screen.

beats.scene: A small bald man begs the raised axe not to strike
beats.summary: The little man says that he is Oz, but begs them not to hurt him, and admits that he has been making believe.

beats.scene: Four friends stare at a trembling little man who rubs his hands together
beats.summary: Each friend says what Oz looked like to them, and the little man admits that he has been making believe.

beats.scene: A paper head, a lady's dress and animal skins lie in a small room
beats.summary: Oz shows them his tricks: the paper head on a wire, his ventriloquist voice, a lady's mask, a beast of skins and a ball of cotton.

beats.scene: The little man sits in a chair and tells his story to five listeners
beats.summary: Oz tells them that he was born in Omaha, learned to be a ventriloquist and then became a balloonist.

beats.scene: A big balloon with a small basket floats over a strange green country
beats.summary: One day his balloon's ropes twisted, and a wind carried him for a day and a night to a strange and beautiful country.

beats.scene: People kneel before a man who steps out of a basket
beats.summary: The people thought he was a great Wizard, and he let them build the Emerald City and put green spectacles on everyone.

beats.scene: A small wizard looks out a palace window, afraid of distant witches
beats.summary: Oz explains that he hid in his palace because he feared the Witches, until Dorothy killed them, and then he cannot keep his promises.

beats.scene: Dorothy frowns at the little man while the Scarecrow listens closely
beats.summary: Dorothy calls him a very bad man, but Oz says he is a good man and a very bad Wizard.

beats.scene: A green bottle and a silk heart sit on a small shelf
beats.summary: He promises to give the Lion courage and the Woodman a heart, and Dorothy asks how she will get home.

beats.scene: Oz measures bran and pins and needles into a bowl beside the Scarecrow
beats.summary: The next morning Oz takes off the Scarecrow's head and stuffs it with bran, pins and needles, and fills the rest with straw.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman receives a heart of silk and sawdust through a square patch
beats.summary: Oz cuts a hole in the Tin Woodman's chest, puts in a silk heart stuffed with sawdust and covers it with a patch.

beats.scene: Dorothy sits sadly at a green window while her friends try to cheer her
beats.summary: For three days Oz sends no word, and Dorothy feels sad and lonely, though her friends are happy with their gifts.

beats.scene: Dorothy and Oz talk beside a roll of green silk
beats.summary: On the fourth day Oz sends for her and says he has found a way to cross the desert: a balloon.

beats.scene: Dorothy sews long strips of green silk beside Oz at a big table
beats.summary: Oz will make the balloon of silk coated with glue and fill it with hot air, and he decides to go with her.

beats.scene: Dorothy sews while Oz cuts silk of light, dark and emerald green
beats.summary: They sew strips of light, dark and emerald silk for three days, and Oz paints the balloon with glue.

beats.scene: A clothes basket tied with many ropes hangs under the green balloon
beats.summary: Oz fastens a big clothes basket to the balloon with many ropes and tells his people that he is visiting a brother Wizard in the clouds.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman builds a fire while a crowd watches a green balloon fill
beats.summary: The balloon is carried out in front of the palace, and the Tin Woodman builds a fire to fill it with hot air.

beats.scene: Oz stands in the basket and speaks to the crowd beside the Scarecrow
beats.summary: Oz gets into the basket and tells the people that the Scarecrow will rule while he is gone.

beats.scene: Dorothy lifts Toto from a crowd as a kitten runs away
beats.summary: Dorothy cannot find Toto, who has run into the crowd to bark at a kitten, and she picks him up and runs for the balloon.

beats.scene: The balloon rises into the sky as Dorothy holds Toto and screams
beats.summary: The ropes snap and the balloon rises without Dorothy, who cries out for it to come back.

beats.scene: The people look up at a tiny balloon in the sky
beats.summary: That is the last that anyone sees of Oz, though the people remember him lovingly and mourn for him, and Dorothy weeps.

beats.scene: Dorothy cries on a green sofa while the Tin Woodman tries to comfort her
beats.summary: Dorothy weeps over the lost chance of going home, and her friends try to comfort her.

beats.scene: A soldier with a long green beard speaks to the Scarecrow and Dorothy
beats.summary: The soldier with the green whiskers suggests Glinda, the Good Witch of the South, who may know a way to cross the desert.

beats.scene: Dorothy hugs the green soldier at the palace door while the friends wait
beats.summary: Dorothy decides to go, her friends will go with her, and they say goodbye to the soldier and walk south.

beats.scene: Dorothy and her friends walk through sunny fields of flowers and fruit trees
beats.summary: They walk through pleasant fields toward the south, until they come to a thick forest.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow reaches under the branches of a huge tree and is seized
beats.summary: The Scarecrow walks up to the first tree, and its branches bend down, seize him and throw him back.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman chops the branch of an angry tree with his axe
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman chops the branch that seizes him, and the tree shakes in pain.

beats.scene: A tall smooth white china wall rises across the road, with no door
beats.summary: The other trees do not move, and beyond them they come to a high wall of white china.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman builds a long ladder from a fallen tree beside the wall
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman makes a ladder out of wood from the Fighting Trees.

beats.scene: Dorothy and her friends climb the ladder up the white china wall
beats.summary: They climb the ladder, and from the top of the wall they see the China Country below.

beats.scene: Tiny china people with painted faces stand among china cows and houses
beats.summary: In the China Country everything is made of china, even the people, and Dorothy walks carefully so as not to break anyone.

beats.scene: The Lion's tail knocks over a little china church
beats.summary: They leave the China Country before they do more damage, and climb down the wall.

beats.scene: Dorothy and her friends enter a thick forest full of watchful animals
beats.summary: Beyond the wall they enter a forest full of wild animals, who are gathered for a meeting.

beats.scene: A huge tiger bows before the Lion while hundreds of animals look on
beats.summary: The animals greet the Lion as the King of Beasts and ask him to kill a great monster that is destroying them.

beats.scene: The Lion crouches in front of a gigantic sleeping spider in a dark forest
beats.summary: The Lion agrees, and he finds the monster asleep and kills it with a single blow.

beats.scene: The beasts of the forest kneel around the Lion, who wears a proud smile
beats.summary: The animals make the Lion their King, and he promises to return when Dorothy has gone home.

beats.scene: A steep rocky hill with strange people on top
beats.summary: The forest ends at a steep, rocky hill, and they see strange people with flat heads standing at the top.

beats.scene: A flat-headed Hammer-Head shoots his head out on a long neck toward the friends
beats.summary: A Hammer-Head's head shoots out on a long neck, and the friends run back, for it is no use to fight them.

beats.scene: Winged Monkeys carry Dorothy and her friends high above the Hammer-Heads' hill
beats.summary: Dorothy uses the Golden Cap a second time, and the Winged Monkeys carry them over the hill.

beats.scene: Round red houses and red fences line the road in a country of red
beats.summary: They reach the country of the Quadlings, where all the houses and fields are red and the people are kind.

beats.scene: Dorothy and her friends stand before a red castle with soldiers in red uniforms
beats.summary: At Glinda's castle, soldiers in red ask them why they have come, and the travelers say they wish to see the Good Witch.

beats.scene: Glinda sits on a ruby throne in a bright hall, smiling at the visitors
beats.summary: Glinda, young and beautiful, sits on a ruby throne and asks Dorothy what she can do for her.

beats.scene: Dorothy tells her story to Glinda beside a window in a red hall
beats.summary: Dorothy tells Glinda how the cyclone brought her to Oz, and says that she wants to go back to Kansas.

beats.scene: Glinda kisses Dorothy's cheek and holds out her hand for the Golden Cap
beats.summary: Glinda kisses her and says she knows a way, but she asks for the Golden Cap, and Dorothy gives it gladly.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow stands before Glinda, who smiles at his painted face
beats.summary: Glinda asks the Scarecrow what he will do, and he says that he will go back to rule the Emerald City.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman leans on his axe in Glinda's red hall and thinks
beats.summary: The Tin Woodman says that he will rule the Winkies, and Glinda says that she will send the Monkeys to take him there.

beats.scene: The Lion shakes his shaggy mane as Glinda looks at him with a smile
beats.summary: The Lion says that he will go back to the forest, and Glinda promises that the third command will take him there and that the Monkeys will then be free.

beats.scene: The Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Lion bow low before Glinda
beats.summary: The friends thank Glinda, and Dorothy asks again how she can get back to Kansas.

beats.scene: Glinda points to the silver shoes on Dorothy's feet in a bright hall
beats.summary: Glinda says that the silver shoes will carry Dorothy over the desert, and she could have gone home the first day.

beats.scene: The three friends talk happily in the red hall
beats.summary: The friends say that they are glad Dorothy did not know, because then they would not have their brains, heart and courage.

beats.scene: Dorothy smiles at her three friends and lifts one silver shoe in the air
beats.summary: Dorothy is glad she helped them, and Glinda explains that the shoes carry a wearer anywhere in three steps if the heels are knocked together.

beats.scene: Dorothy throws her arms around the Lion's neck and pats his big head
beats.summary: Dorothy throws her arms around the Lion's neck, kisses him and pats his big head.

beats.scene: The Tin Woodman weeps beside Dorothy, who wipes his tears carefully
beats.summary: She kisses the Tin Woodman, who weeps in a way most dangerous to his joints, and she hugs the Scarecrow.

beats.scene: Glinda the Good steps down from her ruby throne to kiss Dorothy
beats.summary: Glinda steps down from her ruby throne and gives Dorothy a goodbye kiss, and Dorothy thanks her.

beats.scene: Dorothy holds Toto solemnly in her arms and raises her silver heels
beats.summary: Dorothy takes Toto in her arms, says one last goodbye and clicks her heels three times, asking to be taken home to Aunt Em.

beats.scene: A swirl of wind lifts Dorothy and Toto high above Oz
beats.summary: Instantly she is whirled through the air so fast that she can only hear the wind in her ears.

beats.scene: Dorothy rolls over and over on the grass of the wide Kansas prairie
beats.summary: The shoes stop suddenly, and Dorothy rolls over on the grass of the Kansas prairie.

beats.scene: A new farmhouse stands on the Kansas prairie where the old one was
beats.summary: Just in front of her is the new farmhouse that Uncle Henry built after the cyclone carried away the old one.

beats.scene: Dorothy stands in stocking feet as Toto runs barking toward the barn
beats.summary: Uncle Henry is milking the cows, and Toto runs to the barn, while Dorothy finds that the silver shoes fell off and are lost in the desert.

beats.scene: Aunt Em runs from the farmhouse with open arms and wet cabbages behind her
beats.summary: Aunt Em has just come out of the house to water the cabbages, and she looks up and sees Dorothy running toward her.

beats.scene: Dorothy hugs Aunt Em in the Kansas sunshine while Toto jumps around them
beats.summary: Dorothy answers that she has come from the Land of Oz, and says that she is so glad to be at home again.

A1A2: Dorothy lived on a big, flat prairie in Kansas with her little dog Toto.
The house was small, with one room, a stove, a table and two beds.
The sun and wind had made Aunt Em and Uncle Henry gray too.
One day Uncle Henry looked at the sky and saw it grow dark.
The tall grass bent in waves, and Uncle Henry ran to the animals.
Aunt Em opened the trap door and called Dorothy to the cellar.
Dorothy caught Toto, but the house shook and she fell down.
The house turned around twice and then rose slowly into the air.
Dorothy lay on her bed with Toto, and soon she fell asleep.
A sudden bump woke her, and bright sunshine came through the window.
Dorothy opened the door and saw a very beautiful green country.
There were tall fruit trees, bright flowers, singing birds and a little river.
Three small men and one old woman walked slowly toward the house.
The old woman thanked Dorothy for killing the Wicked Witch of the East.
Dorothy said there was a mistake, because she had not killed anyone.
The old woman pointed to two feet in silver shoes under the house.
For many years the Wicked Witch had made the Munchkins work as slaves.
Dorothy wanted to go home, but the old woman said there was no road.
The old witch told Dorothy to ask the Great Wizard of Oz for help.
The old witch spun around on one toe three times and was gone.
Dorothy washed her face, put on her clean dress, and took her basket.
She found the yellow road and walked along it with Toto.
Round blue houses stood beside the road, and the farmers waved to her.
At night she came to a big house where many people were dancing.
A rich man named Boq asked Dorothy to stay at his house.
Dorothy sat at the long table and ate a very big supper.
Boq asked where she was going, and she told him about the Wizard.
Dorothy slept well in a soft bed, and Toto slept on a rug.
In the morning Dorothy ate breakfast, thanked Boq and started walking again.
Not far away, Dorothy saw a scarecrow on a pole in a field.
The Scarecrow winked at Dorothy and said good day in a soft voice.
Dorothy lifted the Scarecrow off his pole, and he was very light.
The Scarecrow shook himself and said he felt like a new man.
Dorothy told him she was going to the Emerald City to see Oz.
He said he had no brains, because his head was stuffed with straw.
He asked to go with her and ask the Wizard for some brains.
A brick was missing from the road, and the Scarecrow fell on his face.
The Scarecrow could not see why Dorothy wanted to leave this lovely country.
At night they found a small house, and Dorothy ate some bread.
In the morning they walked on and came to a dark forest.
Deep in the forest, they heard a sad sound near the road.
They found a man made of tin, standing still with his axe up.
His body could not move, but his eyes looked at Dorothy and the Scarecrow.
Dorothy ran to the little house and brought back an oil can.
She oiled his neck, his arms and his legs, and he began to move.
The Tin Woodman thanked them, and he said he would have stood there forever.
He said he would like to ask the Wizard for a heart.
He was once a woodman, and he loved a pretty Munchkin girl.
The old woman did not want to lose the girl, so she asked a witch.
A tinsmith made him a new leg out of tin.
The axe cut off his other leg, his arms and his head.
At last he was made all of tin, but he had no heart.
The rain made him rust, and he stood in the forest for a year.
The Woodman asked to come with them to ask Oz for a heart.
The Tin Woodman took his axe and his oil can and went with them.
The Tin Woodman stepped on a beetle, and he cried because he was sorry.
At night they camped under a tree, and the Scarecrow found nuts.
A great Lion jumped out of the trees with a loud roar.
The Lion hit the Tin Woodman, but the tin was too hard for him.
Dorothy ran up and slapped the Lion hard on his big nose.
The Lion said he had not bitten Toto, but Dorothy called him a coward.
The Lion cried, because he was born a coward and could not change.
The Lion said his heart beat fast, and the Tin Woodman smiled.
The Lion joined them, and he jumped over a wide ditch with each friend.
The forest grew darker, and the Lion told them about the Kalidahs.
They came to another ditch, too wide for the Lion to jump.
The Tin Woodman cut the tree down, and it made a bridge.
As they crossed, two Kalidahs ran out of the forest after them.
The Tin Woodman chopped the tree, and the Kalidahs fell into the ditch.
Beyond the forest was a wide river, so they built a raft.
The pole stuck in the mud, and the Scarecrow hung in the middle of the river.
The Lion swam and pulled the raft, and the friends came to the bank.
A big bird flew down, took the Scarecrow and flew him to the bank.
They came to a field of bright red flowers called poppies.
Dorothy and Toto lay down in the flowers, and the Lion lay down too.
The Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow carried Dorothy and Toto out of the field.
The Tin Woodman chased a big yellow cat away from a mouse.
The mouse was the Queen of the Field Mice, and she wanted to help them.
Hundreds of mice came, and they pulled the sleeping Lion out of the field.
The Lion woke up, and the Queen said she would come if called.
As they walked, they saw green houses, green fences and green clothes.
At night they slept by the road, and the sky glowed green.
In the morning they saw a high green wall with a gate full of emeralds.
A small green man opened the gate and asked what they wanted.
He said everyone must wear green glasses, or the light would hurt their eyes.
He put green glasses on everyone, even Toto, and locked them with a key.
They walked through streets of tall green houses that shone with emeralds.
In the shops they saw green sweets, green shoes, and happy children.
A soldier with a long green beard opened the palace door.
A green girl took Dorothy to a pretty room and gave her a green dress.
In the morning Dorothy went into a big room and saw a huge head.
The head said it was Oz, the Great and Terrible, and asked her name.
Oz said Dorothy must kill the Wicked Witch of the West, and she cried.
The next day the Scarecrow saw a lovely lady with wings on the throne.
The Tin Woodman saw a terrible beast and asked it for a heart.
The Lion saw a ball of fire and asked it for courage.
The friends met and found that each had seen a different Oz.
They decided to go and find the Witch, but the Lion was afraid.
In the morning the Guardian told them to go west, where the sun sets.
They left the city, and Dorothy's green dress was white now.
The Wicked Witch had one big eye, and she saw the friends far away.
A pack of wolves came running when the Witch blew her whistle.
The Tin Woodman fought the wolves with his axe, one after another.
The Witch saw the dead wolves, and she called a great flock of crows.
The Scarecrow fought the crows alone and beat every one of them.
Then the Witch sent a swarm of black bees to sting them.
The bees tried to sting the Tin Woodman, but his tin was too hard.
The Witch sent her Winkies, but the Lion roared and they ran away.
The Witch took out the Golden Cap, which could call the Winged Monkeys.
The Witch called the Winged Monkeys and told them to find Dorothy.
The Monkeys dropped the Tin Woodman on rocks and threw the Scarecrow's straw away.
The rest of the Monkeys tied the Lion up with ropes and carried him away.
The Monkey King could not hurt Dorothy, because of the kiss on her head.
The Witch was afraid of Dorothy's silver shoes, but she hid her fear.
The Witch took Dorothy to the kitchen and gave her hard work.
The Lion would not work for the Witch, so Dorothy brought him food.
Dorothy tripped on an iron bar, and one silver shoe fell off.
Dorothy was so angry that she threw a bucket of water over the Witch.
The Witch cried out and melted away into a brown puddle on the floor.
Dorothy cleaned the floor and put her silver shoe back on her foot.
Dorothy told the Lion the Witch was dead, and he was free.
The Winkies came out and thanked them, because they were free now.
The Winkies helped Dorothy find the Tin Woodman on the rocks.
Some Winkies were tinsmiths, and they worked for three days on him.
The Tin Woodman was fixed, and he cried happily when he thanked Dorothy.
They found the Scarecrow's clothes at the top of a very tall tree.
The Tin Woodman cut down the tree, and the clothes fell to the ground.
The Winkies filled the Scarecrow with fresh straw, and he was happy again.
The Winkies asked the Tin Woodman to be their ruler, but he said no.
Dorothy found the Golden Cap, and the friends started back to the city.
The friends walked east, but they lost their way.
Dorothy remembered the Golden Cap, and she said the magic words.
She asked the Monkeys to take them to the Emerald City.
On the way the Monkey King told Dorothy why the Monkeys must obey the Cap.
His grandfather dropped a young man into a river as a joke.
The Monkeys put them down at the gate, and the Guardian was surprised.
Oz would not see them, though they waited for four days.
At last Oz agreed to see them, and they went into the Throne Room.
The Lion roared, and Toto knocked over a screen in the corner.
The little man said he was Oz, but he asked them not to hurt him.
Each friend said what Oz had looked like, and the man said he was a humbug.
Oz showed them his tricks, the paper head and the mask and the cotton fire.
Oz said he came from Omaha and that he once went up in balloons.
One day his balloon flew far away and came down in a strange country.
The people thought he was a great Wizard, so he had them build a city.
Oz said he hid in his palace because he was afraid of the Witches.
Dorothy called him a bad man, but he said he was only a bad Wizard.
Oz promised the Lion courage and the Tin Woodman a heart.
Oz filled the Scarecrow's head with bran, pins and needles.
Oz put a silk heart in the Tin Woodman, and the Lion drank from a bottle.
For three days Dorothy waited for news, and she was sad.
On the fourth day Oz told Dorothy that he had found a way, a balloon.
Oz said they would make a balloon of silk, and he would go with her.
They sewed green silk for three days, and it made a big green bag.
Oz tied a basket to the balloon and told the people he was leaving.
The Tin Woodman made a big fire, and the balloon began to fill up.
Oz got into the basket and said the Scarecrow would rule while he was away.
Toto ran after a kitten, and Dorothy went to find him.
The ropes snapped, and the balloon flew up without Dorothy.
No one saw Oz again, but the people remembered him with love.
Dorothy cried because she had lost her way home, and her friends tried to help.
The soldier told them that Glinda, the Good Witch of the South, might help.
Dorothy decided to go to Glinda, and her friends went with her.
They walked through sunny fields until they came to a thick forest.
The Scarecrow went to the first tree, and the branches seized him.
The Tin Woodman cut the branch with his axe, and the tree shook.
Beyond the trees there was a high white wall made of china.
The Tin Woodman made a tall ladder out of wood.
They climbed the ladder, and from the top they saw a strange land.
In the China Country everything was china, even the cows and the people.
They left the China Country, and the Lion's tail knocked over a little church.
Beyond the wall they entered a dark forest full of wild animals.
A tiger told the Lion that a great monster was hurting the animals.
The Lion found the monster asleep and killed it with one blow.
The animals made the Lion their King, and he said he would come back.
At the end of the forest was a steep hill, with strange people at the top.
A Hammer-Head's head shot out on a long neck, and they ran back.
Dorothy called the Winged Monkeys, and they carried the friends over the hill.
They came to the country of the Quadlings, where everything was red.
At the red castle, soldiers asked why they had come to see Glinda.
Glinda was young and beautiful, and she asked how she could help.
Dorothy told Glinda her story and said she wanted to go home.
Glinda said she knew a way, but she asked for the Golden Cap.
The Scarecrow said he would go back to the Emerald City and rule.
The Tin Woodman said he would go back and rule the kind Winkies.
The Lion said he would go to his forest, and Glinda promised to send him.
The friends thanked Glinda, and Dorothy asked how she could get to Kansas.
Glinda said the silver shoes could carry Dorothy home across the desert.
The friends said they were glad, because they now had brains, a heart and courage.
Dorothy was glad she had helped them, and she wished to go home now.
Dorothy put her arms around the Lion's neck and kissed him.
She kissed the Tin Woodman, who cried, and she hugged the Scarecrow.
Glinda stepped down from her throne and kissed Dorothy goodbye.
Dorothy picked up Toto and said goodbye one last time.
At once the wind lifted her and carried her through the air.
Then she stopped so suddenly that she rolled over on the grass.
Before her stood the new farmhouse that Uncle Henry had built.
Toto ran to the barn, and Dorothy saw that her silver shoes were gone.
Aunt Em came out to water the cabbages and saw Dorothy running to her.
Dorothy said she came from Oz, and she was so happy to be home.
B1B2: Dorothy is a small girl who lives in the middle of the great Kansas prairie. She has no brothers or sisters, but she has a little black dog called Toto.

The farmhouse has only one room, and the boards of its walls were carried there by wagon from far away. In the floor there is a trap door, and under it a small hole where the family can hide from storms.
Years of hard work and burning sun have turned the grass, the house and even the grown-ups gray. Uncle Henry never laughs, and only Toto can make Dorothy smile.
One afternoon Uncle Henry sits by the door and looks anxiously at the sky. It is darker than usual, and he can hear a low wail of wind far away.
The long grass bends in waves in front of the storm, and Uncle Henry shouts that a cyclone is coming. Then he runs to the barn to save the cows and horses.
One look at the sky tells Aunt Em all she needs to know. She opens the trap door in the floor, climbs down the ladder and calls for Dorothy to follow.

Toto jumps out of Dorothy's arms and hides under the bed in terror, so she kneels down and catches him. Just as she runs for the trap door, the whole house gives a great shake, and she sits down hard on the floor.
Then something strange happens: the house whirls around two or three times and rises slowly into the air. Dorothy feels as if she is going up in a balloon.
It is very dark, and the wind howls around the house, but Dorothy finds that she is riding quite gently. After a few hours she lies down on her bed with Toto beside her and falls asleep.
Hours later, a sudden shock wakes Dorothy, and she sits up in surprise. Sunshine is pouring through the window, and the house is no longer moving.
Dorothy jumps off her bed, opens the door and cannot believe her eyes. Outside there is a lovely country, nothing like the gray prairie she knows.
The cyclone has set the house down in the middle of a country of rare beauty. There are green lawns, fruit trees heavy with ripe fruit, and birds of strange bright colors singing in the branches.
While Dorothy is still staring, she sees a group of strange people coming toward her. There are three men and a woman, and the men are no taller than she is.
The old woman bows to Dorothy and welcomes her to the land of the Munchkins. She thanks her for killing the Wicked Witch of the East and setting her people free.
Dorothy is very puzzled, because she has never killed anything in her life. She explains politely that a cyclone carried her here, so there must be some mistake.
The old woman laughs and points to the corner of the house. Two feet stick out from under the heavy wooden beam, and they are wearing shining silver shoes.
The old woman explains that the Witch of the East kept the Munchkins as slaves for many years, day and night. Now they are free, and they are grateful to the girl who has freed them.

Dorothy says that her Aunt Em will be worried, and she asks the old woman how to get home to Kansas. The Witch of the North shakes her head, because deserts surround the whole country, and no one has crossed them.
The old woman says that the only person who can help is the Great Oz, who lives in the Emerald City. Then she kisses Dorothy gently on the forehead, leaving a round, shining mark.
The Witch gives Dorothy the dead witch's silver shoes and says they have a powerful charm. Then she spins around three times on her heel and vanishes, leaving Dorothy to pack her basket.
Dorothy is dusty and tired, so she washes her face and puts on a clean blue-and-white dress. Then she fills her basket with bread, ties on her sunbonnet and calls Toto.
It is easy to find the road of yellow brick, and soon Dorothy is walking along it with Toto trotting at her heels. The silver shoes ring merrily on the hard yellow stones.
On both sides of the road, there are neat blue fences and round blue houses with dome roofs. Munchkin farmers look up from their fields and bow low as the girl who killed the Wicked Witch goes by.
As evening comes and her feet begin to ache, Dorothy reaches a larger house than any she has seen. On the green lawn in front, many Munchkins are dancing and laughing.
A rich Munchkin called Boq steps forward and welcomes Dorothy warmly. He invites her to stay the night, because she has killed the Wicked Witch of the East.
Boq seats Dorothy near the head of the table and she eats as much as she can. The Munchkins watch her with great curiosity, and they stare at her silver shoes.
Boq asks Dorothy where she is going, and she says she wants the Great Oz to send her home from the Emerald City. Boq tells her that Oz is very powerful and that he himself has never seen him.
After supper Boq shows Dorothy to a pretty room with a soft bed and clean white sheets. She falls asleep at once, while Toto curls up on a blue rug at her feet.
In the morning, Dorothy eats a good breakfast and watches a tiny Munchkin baby play with Toto. Then she thanks Boq for his kindness and sets out along the road once more.
A few miles from Boq's house, Dorothy sees a cornfield and a scarecrow high on a pole. He has a painted face and a pointed blue hat, and she thinks he is looking at her.
Dorothy is sure that one of the painted eyes slowly winks at her. Then the scarecrow nods in a friendly way and says good day, and he complains that it is tiresome to stand there all day.
The Scarecrow cannot get down, because the pole is pushed up his back. Dorothy reaches up, lifts him off, and finds that he is as light as a feather, because he is stuffed with straw.
The Scarecrow bows, shakes himself and pats his body to put the straw back in place. He declares that he feels like a new man, and then he asks who Dorothy is.
Dorothy tells him that her name is Dorothy and that she is walking to the Emerald City. She hopes that the great Oz will send her back to Kansas, and the Scarecrow asks who Oz is.
The Scarecrow says that his head is filled with straw instead of brains. A Munchkin farmer made him only two days ago, and an old crow soon told him what was wrong with him.
The Scarecrow does not mind having a stuffed body, because nothing can hurt it, but he hates to be called a fool. Dorothy kindly invites him to come with her and ask Oz for brains.
At first Toto does not trust the Scarecrow and sniffs at his straw suspiciously. Soon the Scarecrow trips over a hole in the road where a brick is missing, but he laughs and gets up unhurt.

The Scarecrow does not understand why Dorothy wants to leave this beautiful country for the dry gray land she calls Kansas. She replies that it is because he has no brains, for home is home, however gray it may be.

When night falls they find a small farmhouse beside the road, and they go in to rest. Dorothy shares her bread with Toto and goes to sleep, while the Scarecrow stands in a corner and waits for morning.
In the morning Dorothy washes in a brook, eats a little bread and sets out again with her friends. Soon the yellow road enters a thick forest, and the trees grow darker overhead.
Deep in the forest, the travelers hear a low groan coming from somewhere close by. Dorothy jumps and Toto growls, but the Scarecrow says they should go and look.
Behind some trees they find a man made entirely of tin, standing as still as a statue. His axe is raised against a tree trunk, and his bright eyes are looking at them.

Dorothy asks whether he groaned, and the tin man says that he did, and that he has been groaning for more than a year. He cannot move, but his eyes follow them, and he begs them to fetch an oil can from his cottage.
Dorothy hurries along the path to the little cottage where the Woodman lives, and she finds the oil can on a shelf. She runs back and asks him where to put the oil first.
Dorothy oils his neck, and the Scarecrow moves his head gently from side to side until it works smoothly. Then she oils his arms and legs, and at last he can lower his axe and lean it against a tree.

The Tin Woodman thanks Dorothy and the Scarecrow with all his heart, for he would have stood there forever without them. He says that they have saved his life, and he wants to know how they happened to come.
Dorothy explains that they are going to see the Great Oz, and the Tin Woodman says that he would like a heart. He sits on a log to tell them why, because he once had a heart.

Long ago the Tin Woodman was a real man, the son of a woodman, who cut down trees for his living. After his father died he took care of his old mother, and he fell in love with a beautiful Munchkin girl.
The old woman who kept the girl did not want to lose her, because the girl did all the housework. She went to the Wicked Witch of the East, and the Witch promised to enchant the woodman's axe.
At first the woodman thinks this is a terrible misfortune, since a one-legged man cannot work well. A clever tinsmith makes him a new leg from tin, and he goes back to work and is happy again.
The axe slips again and again, and it cuts off his other leg, then his arms, and then his head. Each time the clever tinsmith replaces the missing part with a new one made of tin.
At last the axe cuts his body in half, and the tinsmith joins two tin pieces together. Now the Woodman is made of tin from head to foot, but his real heart has gone, and he no longer loves the girl.
One day a heavy storm of rain catches the Woodman in the middle of his work and rusts his joints. He stands there for a whole year until Dorothy comes, and he longs to have a heart.
The Tin Woodman says that he would rather have a heart than anything else in the world. The Scarecrow says that brains are better, but the Woodman answers that a heart makes people truly happy.
Dorothy cannot decide which of the two is right, but she agrees to take the Woodman with her. He picks up his axe and fills his oil can from his cottage, and they all set out together.
The Woodman steps on a small beetle by accident, and he starts to cry bitter tears. His jaws rust shut, and Dorothy has to oil them again so that he can speak.
At night they rest under a big tree, and Dorothy has only a little bread left. The Scarecrow fills her basket with nuts, and the Tin Woodman cuts wood for a fire.
In the dark of the night the friends hear a fearful roar, and a great Lion leaps out of the trees. With one blow of his paw he sends the Scarecrow spinning over and over to the edge of the road.
Next, the Lion strikes the Tin Woodman with his sharp claws, but the tin does not break, and the Lion hurts his paw. Then he turns on Toto, and Toto runs at him, barking.
Dorothy feels that Toto will be killed, so she rushes forward and slaps the Lion as hard as she can on his nose. The huge beast sits down, rubs his nose with his paw and begins to cry.
The Lion says he did not bite Toto, but Dorothy answers that he tried. She tells him that he is nothing but a big coward, to attack a little dog and a poor stuffed man.
The Lion explains that he is the King of the Beasts, so everyone expects him to be brave. When he meets any danger, his heart beats fast, but he roars so loudly that everything runs away.

The Lion says that when danger comes, his heart beats fast, and the Tin Woodman suggests that he may have heart disease. If that is true, the Woodman says, the Lion should be glad, because it proves that he has a heart.

The Lion asks if he may travel with them, and he promises to ask the Wizard for courage. In the morning the friends come to a deep ditch across the road, and the Lion carries each friend over it, one by one.
The forest grows darker, and strange growls come from the trees. The Lion says that the Kalidahs live there, beasts with bodies like bears and heads like tigers, and they are not afraid of him.
Soon they reach another ditch, wider and deeper than the first, and the Lion cannot jump it. The Scarecrow looks at a big tree that grows near the edge, and he has a clever idea.
The Tin Woodman chops at the tree with his axe, and soon it begins to totter. With a loud crash it falls across the ditch, and its top branches lie on the far side to make a bridge.
As the Scarecrow leads the way across the tree trunk, a growl makes them turn around. Two fierce Kalidahs are bounding toward them, and the Lion says that they must hurry.
The Lion crosses last, and the Kalidahs are already on the tree trunk behind him. The Tin Woodman raises his axe, chops the tree through, and the beasts tumble down into the ditch.
At last they leave the forest behind, and they see a wide, swift river across their road. The Tin Woodman builds a raft from logs, and the friends stand on it, ready to sail across.

On the raft, the Scarecrow pushes with a long pole, but the river is deep and the current is strong. The pole sticks fast in the mud, and the raft sails away and leaves him hanging in the middle of the river.
The raft floats down the river, and the Lion jumps in and swims to the shore with the raft behind him. Dorothy and the Tin Woodman push with the pole, and at last they all reach the bank.
The friends walk along the bank, and they see a stork flying near the Scarecrow, who calls out to it. The stork lifts the stuffed man from his pole with its claws and carries him to the shore.
Soon the friends come to a wide field of bright red poppies that stretches as far as they can see. The flowers are so beautiful that Dorothy cries out with joy, and she walks into the field.
Before long, Dorothy's eyes grow heavy, and she cannot keep them open. The Tin Woodman tells her to run, but she lies down in the poppies, and the Lion and Toto fall asleep beside her.

The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman are not made of flesh, so the poppies do not harm them. They pick up Dorothy and her little dog, carry them out of the flowers and lay them on soft grass by the river.
While the two friends wait, a wildcat dashes past with a tiny mouse running before it. The kind Tin Woodman raises his axe and chases the wildcat away, and the mouse stops to thank him.
The little mouse is the Queen of all the Field Mice, and she bows to the Tin Woodman. She promises to help in any way she can, and the Scarecrow asks if her people can save the Lion.
The Queen calls her people, and hundreds of mice run up from all sides. The Tin Woodman makes a little wooden truck, they put the Lion on it, and the mice pull him out of the field of poppies.
At last the Lion wakes, safe and sound, and he is delighted to be alive. The Queen of the Mice bows goodbye, and she promises to come when they call, if they ever need her again.
As the friends walk on, the country grows more and more green. The fences, houses and even the clothes of the people they meet are all a bright shade of green.
That night the friends sleep under a large tree beside the road, for there is no house nearby. Before they close their eyes, they notice that the sky ahead shines with a strange green glow.
The next morning, Dorothy sees a high, thick wall of green in front of them. In the middle of it stands a big gate set with shining emeralds, so bright that even the Scarecrow's painted eyes ache.
The big gate swings open, and a little man in green looks at them with wonder. He is the Guardian of the Gates, and he warns them that the Great Oz is terrible when he is angry.
The Guardian tells them that they must put on green spectacles before they enter. The glory of the Emerald City is so bright that it would blind them if they looked at it with their bare eyes.
The Guardian opens a big box filled with spectacles of every size and finds a pair that fits each one. He fastens a gold band behind each head and locks it, and he has the only key.
The Guardian leads them through the gate and into streets lined with beautiful houses. The houses are built of green marble, set with sparkling emeralds, and the pavement shines like green glass.
In the street there are shops where people sell green candy, green popcorn and green shoes. Men and women in green go by, and little children play happily with green balls.
The Guardian takes them to the palace of the Wizard, and a soldier with long green whiskers stands at the gate. He listens to their story and tells them to wait while he asks the Wizard.
The soldier comes back with news that the Wizard will see them tomorrow. Then a pretty green maid takes Dorothy to a bedroom, lays out a green silk dress and ties a green ribbon around Toto's neck.
In the morning the soldier leads Dorothy to a great green hall with a throne in the middle. On the throne sits an enormous head, with no body, no arms and no legs.
A great voice booms that it is Oz, the Great and Terrible, and it asks who she is. The head looks at her silver shoes and the shining mark on her forehead before it asks what she wants.
Oz will send her home only if she first kills the Wicked Witch of the West. Dorothy begins to cry, because she has never killed anything on purpose, and she does not know how to do it.
On the second day the Scarecrow goes into the throne room. He sees a lovely lady in green silk with beautiful wings, and she asks him why he has come.
On the third day the Tin Woodman faces a terrible beast with the head of a rhinoceros and five eyes. He bravely asks for a heart, but the beast also says that he must kill the Wicked Witch first.
On the fourth day the Lion stands in front of a great ball of fire that burns so hot he cannot get close. He asks for courage, but the voice says that he must bring proof that the Witch is dead.
That evening the friends sit together in Dorothy's room and tell each other what they saw. Each of them saw a different Oz, and each of them was told to kill the Witch.

Dorothy says that she cannot go home unless the Witch is destroyed, and the Scarecrow offers to go with her. The Lion says that he is afraid, but he promises to go, and the Woodman says he will do anything for a heart.

The next morning the soldier takes them to the Guardian, who unlocks their spectacles and explains the way. No road goes to the West, he says, but if they keep walking toward the setting sun, they will find the Wicked Witch.
The travelers thank the Guardian and walk away to the west over fields of soft grass. Dorothy sees that her silk dress is no longer green, but pure white, and so is the ribbon on Toto's neck.
The Wicked Witch of the West has only one eye, but it is as powerful as a telescope. From the door of her castle she looks around and sees Dorothy asleep far away with her friends.
At once a pack of great wolves comes running from every direction. They have long legs, fierce eyes and sharp teeth, and the Witch tells them to go and tear the strangers to pieces.
The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman wake and see the wolves coming. The Woodman tells the Scarecrow to stand behind him, grabs his sharp axe and fights the leader of the pack.

In the morning the Witch sees her dead wolves, and she is angrier than before. She blows her silver whistle twice, and a great flock of wild crows comes flying to her, so thick that it darkens the sky.
The Scarecrow says that this is his battle, so the others lie down. He stands up and waves his arms, and when the crows fly at him, he catches them and wrings their necks, one at a time.
The Witch is furious, so she calls a swarm of black bees. She orders them to go and sting the strangers to death, and they come buzzing across the sky like a cloud.
The Tin Woodman tells the Scarecrow to scatter his straw over Dorothy, Toto and the Lion. The bees cannot sting them, and when they sting the Woodman, they break their stingers and fall dead.

Dorothy and the Lion get up, and they help the Woodman put the straw back into the Scarecrow. The Witch, who is angrier than ever, sends a band of her Winkie slaves, but the Lion roars and they run away.
Then the Witch takes out her magic Golden Cap, set with diamonds and rubies. Whoever owns the cap can command the Winged Monkeys three times, and she has already used the cap twice.

The Witch puts on the cap and says the magic words, and the sky fills with the noise of wings. The Monkey King bows and asks what she commands, and she orders them to destroy all the strangers except the Lion.
The Monkeys carry the Tin Woodman over a land of sharp rocks and drop him, and he lies badly dented. Others pull the straw out of the Scarecrow and throw his clothes into a very tall tree.

The rest of the Monkeys throw strong ropes around the Lion, winding them so tightly that he cannot bite or scratch. They lift him up, carry him to the Witch's castle and put him in a yard with a high iron fence.
The Monkey King looks at Dorothy and sees the shining mark on her forehead. He says that the Power of Good is greater than the Power of Evil, so they can only carry her to the castle.

The Witch sees the mark on Dorothy's forehead, and then she sees the silver shoes and begins to tremble. Then she looks into Dorothy's eyes and sees how simple the soul behind them is, and she laughs.
The Witch takes Dorothy to a big kitchen and tells her to clean the pots, sweep the floor and keep the fire alive. Dorothy does as she is told, for she is afraid.
The Witch goes to the courtyard to harness the Lion, but he roars so fiercely that she runs away. She says he will have no food until he obeys, but every night Dorothy brings him some food in secret.

The Witch wants the silver shoes, but she is afraid of the dark and of water, so she never goes near Dorothy at night. She sets a trap, hiding an iron bar in the kitchen with magic, and Dorothy trips over it, and one shoe comes off.

Dorothy demands her shoe back, but the Witch says that she will keep it, and she means to take the other one too. In a rage, Dorothy picks up a bucket of water and throws it over the Witch from head to foot.
As Dorothy looks on in wonder, the Witch begins to shrink and melt away like brown sugar. She screams that she did not know that water is the end of her, and she says goodbye to her wicked deeds.
Dorothy throws another bucket of water over the mess and sweeps it all out of the door. She picks up her silver shoe, which is all that is left of the Witch, and wipes it clean and puts it on.
Dorothy runs to the courtyard and opens the gate of the iron fence. She tells the Lion that the Wicked Witch of the West has come to an end, and that they are no longer prisoners.
The yellow Winkies, who were the Witch's slaves for many years, come out into the yard. They cheer for Dorothy and the Lion and celebrate the end of the Witch with a feast.
Dorothy asks the Winkies to help her find her friends. They follow the Lion across the rocky country, and they find the Tin Woodman lying bent and dented among the stones.
Dorothy asks whether any of the Winkies are tinsmiths, and several of them say yes. They hammer out the dents and mend the broken places, and they work for three days and four nights.
The Woodman walks about and thanks the Winkies, and he wipes away happy tears. Dorothy carefully dries his eyes and oils his joints so that he will not rust.
The Winkies help the friends search, and at last they see the Scarecrow's blue clothes in a very tall tree. The tree is so smooth that no one can climb it.
The Tin Woodman raises his axe and cuts away at the trunk of the tall tree. In a few minutes it crashes down, and the Scarecrow's clothes fall to the ground, where the Winkies pick them up.
The Winkies stuff the coat and trousers with clean, fresh straw, and the Scarecrow stands up as good as new. He thanks everyone over and over, for he is glad to be himself again.

The Winkies are so grateful that they ask the Tin Woodman to be their ruler, because he is kind and strong. He says that he would be happy to do so, but first he wants to return to the Emerald City and ask for his heart.
Before they leave, Dorothy finds the Golden Cap in the Witch's cupboard and thinks it is very pretty. She puts it on, says goodbye to the Winkies and sets out toward the east with her friends.
The friends walk toward the east, but there is no road and no path in the Winkies' land. They walk all day, and by evening they know that they are lost.
Dorothy remembers the Golden Cap on her head, and she knows that it is magic. She says the words, and in a moment the Winged Monkeys appear.
Dorothy asks the Monkeys to carry her and her friends to the Emerald City. The King says that it will be done, because they must obey whoever wears the Golden Cap.
While they fly, the Monkey King tells Dorothy about the Monkeys' past. Long ago, he says, they were a free people who lived in a great forest and did exactly as they liked.

Gayelette was a good princess of the North, and she was going to marry a young man named Quelala. The Monkey King's grandfather dropped Quelala into a river as a joke, and his rich clothes were ruined.
The Monkeys set the travelers down gently in front of the gates of the Emerald City and fly away. The Guardian is amazed to see them back, and he cannot believe that the Witch is gone.
The soldier takes the news to Oz, but the Wizard sends back word that he will not see them. They wait for days, and Dorothy begins to cry, while the others grow more and more angry.
On the fifth day the soldier tells them that Oz will see them all together. They hurry to the Throne Room, where an enormous voice asks them what they want.
Oz says he must think about it and tells them to come back tomorrow. The Lion roars so loudly that Toto jumps away, tips over the screen in the corner, and reveals a little old man.
The Tin Woodman raises his axe and asks who the old man is. He says in a trembling voice that he is Oz, the Great and Terrible, but he begs them not to strike him.
