Dorothy thought Oz was a great Head, the Scarecrow a lady, the Tin Woodman a beast and the Lion a ball of fire. The little man meekly answers that he has only been making believe.

Oz leads them to a small room behind the screen and shows them the great Head, made of paper and hung on a wire. He also shows them the lady's dress and mask, the beast made of skins and the ball of cotton.
Oz sits down and tells them that he was born in Omaha, which is not very far from Kansas. He was a ventriloquist at first, and later he became a balloonist who went up on circus days to draw a crowd.

One day the ropes of his balloon get twisted so that he cannot come down, and a current of air carries him many miles away. After a day and a night, he finds himself floating over a strange and beautiful country.
The people see him come down from the clouds and think that he is a great Wizard. He lets them believe it, and he orders them to build the Emerald City and his palace, and to wear green spectacles.

Oz explains that he was always afraid of the Wicked Witches, because they were able to do real magic and he could not. He was glad when Dorothy killed them, but now he must admit that he cannot keep his promises.
Dorothy calls the old man very bad, but he answers that he is a good man and only a bad Wizard. The Scarecrow asks him for brains, and Oz says that he does not need them.

Oz tells the Lion that he already has plenty of courage, because true courage is facing danger when you are afraid. The Lion is not comforted, and Oz agrees to give him some tomorrow, and the same for the Woodman's heart.
The next morning Oz takes off the Scarecrow's head and empties out the straw. He fills it with a mixture of bran, pins and needles, and then he fits the head back onto his shoulders.
Oz cuts a small square hole in the Woodman's chest and puts in a pretty heart made of silk and stuffed with sawdust. Then he gives the Lion a green drink from a bottle, and calls it courage.
Her friends are happy with the gifts that Oz has given them, but Dorothy is sad. For three days she hears nothing from Oz, and she misses Aunt Em and Uncle Henry more than ever.

On the fourth day Oz sends for her and says that he has a plan to take her over the desert. He came to this country in a balloon, so he thinks he can make another balloon, and carry her through the air.

Oz explains that a balloon is made of silk coated with glue to keep the air in, and that he has plenty of silk. There is no gas in this country, so they will fill it with hot air, and Oz will go with Dorothy.

Dorothy takes a needle and thread, and as fast as Oz cuts the silk into strips, she sews them together. First comes a strip of light green, then dark green and then emerald green, and it takes three days.

They need a basket to ride in, so Oz sends the soldier with the green whiskers for a big clothes basket. He fastens it with many ropes to the balloon, and he tells his people that he will visit a brother Wizard in the clouds.

Oz orders the balloon carried to the front of the palace, and the people stare at it with great curiosity. The Tin Woodman has chopped a big pile of wood and he lights it, and Oz holds the mouth of the balloon over the fire.

Oz climbs into the basket, and he tells all the people in a loud voice that he is going away on a visit. While he is gone, he says, the Scarecrow will rule over them, and they must obey him as they would obey Oz.
Oz calls Dorothy to hurry, but she cannot find Toto anywhere. Toto has run into the crowd to bark at a kitten, but she finds him at last and runs toward the balloon.
Just as Dorothy is about to get into the basket, the ropes snap with a crack, and the balloon rises into the air without her. She cries out that she wants to go too, but Oz cannot come back.

That is the last that anyone sees of Oz, the Wonderful Wizard, though he may have reached Omaha safely. The people remember him lovingly and say that he built them this beautiful city and left the Wise Scarecrow to rule them.
Dorothy cries bitterly, because she has lost her chance of ever going home. The Tin Woodman comforts her very carefully, because he knows that his own tears would rust his jaws.
The soldier with the green whiskers says that Glinda, the Good Witch of the South, might help. She is the most powerful of all the Witches, and her castle stands near the desert.

Dorothy decides at once to go to Glinda, and the Lion, the Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow all offer to go with her. The next morning she kisses the green soldier goodbye, and they set off to the south.
For a day they walk through pleasant fields full of flowers and fruit trees, and the sun shines warmly on them. Toward evening they come to a thick forest with no way through or around it.
The Scarecrow goes up to the first tree to find a way between its branches, but the branches bend down and wrap around him. The tree lifts him up and flings him back among his friends.
The Tin Woodman marches up to the next tree and swings his axe. When its branch bends down to seize him, he chops it off, and the tree begins to shake as if it were in pain.
At the other side of the forest, the friends find that the road stops at a high white wall. It is as smooth as the surface of a dish, and it is higher than their heads.
The Tin Woodman goes back to the forest and uses his axe to cut a lot of wood. He builds a tall ladder, and the others wait for him beside the white wall.
The Scarecrow climbs the ladder first, and he cries out in wonder when he reaches the top. Dorothy follows him and cries “Oh my” too, and then the Tin Woodman and Toto come up too.
They find themselves in a land where all the houses, cows, sheep and people are made of china. The friends walk very carefully, because a china person that is broken cannot always be mended.
The friends leave the China Country as carefully as they can, but the Lion's tail knocks over a little china church. They climb back down the wall, glad that they have done so little harm.

Soon they enter a thick forest that is full of wild animals of every kind. The Lion hears a great growling, and when he looks ahead, he sees all the beasts of the forest gathered together in a clearing.
A great tiger bows before the Lion and welcomes him as the King of Beasts. He explains that a terrible monster, like a giant spider, is killing the animals, and he begs the Lion to save them.
The Lion promises to help, and he goes alone to look for the monster. He finds it asleep and so ugly that he almost turns away, but he leaps and kills it with one great blow of his paw.
The Lion walks proudly back to the clearing, and the beasts bow low before him. They ask him to be their King, and the Lion promises to return to rule them as soon as Dorothy is safely home.
At the other side of the forest, they find a high hill covered with rocks. The Scarecrow thinks they can climb it, but a number of strange people stand at the top and look down on them.
When the Scarecrow tries to go forward, a head shoots out on a long neck and knocks him down the hill. The friends run back to the bottom, and they know that they cannot fight such people.
Dorothy puts on the Golden Cap and says the magic words. The Winged Monkeys come, and they carry the travelers over the hill, while the Hammer-Heads look up angrily.
On the other side of the hill, the friends find a beautiful country with red houses and red fields. These are the Quadlings, a plump and good-natured people who live under the Good Witch Glinda.

At the gate of Glinda's castle they find three girls in handsome red uniforms trimmed with gold. One of them asks why they have come, and Dorothy says that they wish to see the Good Witch who rules there.
The girl in red leads the travelers into a grand hall where Glinda sits on a throne of rubies. She is beautiful and young, with red hair, a white dress and blue eyes, and she looks kindly at Dorothy.

Dorothy tells the Witch how the cyclone carried her to Oz, how she met her friends and what adventures they had. She says that she wants only to go back to Kansas, because Aunt Em will think something dreadful has happened.
Glinda leans forward and kisses the sweet face of the loving little girl. She says that she knows a way to get back to Kansas, but she wants the Golden Cap, and Dorothy gives it to her gladly.

Glinda asks the Scarecrow what he will do, and he says that he will rule the Emerald City again. Glinda promises that the Monkeys will carry him to the gates, for the city should not lose so wonderful a ruler.

Glinda asks the Tin Woodman what will become of him, and he answers that the Winkies wanted him to rule them. Glinda promises that the Monkeys will carry him there, and she says that he will rule wisely.
The Lion says that a grand old forest lies over the hill, where all the beasts have made him their King. Glinda promises that her third command will take him there, and then the Monkeys will be free.
The three friends thank the Good Witch, and Dorothy says that she is as good as she is beautiful. But she has not yet said how to get back to Kansas, so Dorothy asks again.
Glinda tells Dorothy that her silver shoes will carry her over the desert. She could have gone back to Aunt Em on the very first day, if she had known their power.
The Scarecrow says that without the long journey he would never have got his brains. The Tin Woodman and the Lion say the same about their heart and their courage.
Dorothy says that she is glad to have helped her friends, and now she would like to go home. Glinda tells her that the shoes can take her anywhere in the world in three steps.
Dorothy runs to the Lion, throws her arms around his neck and kisses him. She pats his big head gently, and the Lion's eyes shine with tears.
Next Dorothy kisses the Tin Woodman, who is weeping in a way that is dangerous to his joints. Then she hugs the soft, stuffed body of the Scarecrow, and she finds that she is crying too.
Glinda the Good steps down from her ruby throne to give the little girl a goodbye kiss. Dorothy thanks her for all the kindness she has shown to her friends and to herself.
Dorothy picks up Toto and holds him tightly in her arms. She says one last goodbye to everyone, claps the heels of her shoes together three times and says, “Take me home to Aunt Em.”

Instantly Dorothy is whirling through the air so quickly that she can only hear the wind whistling past her ears. The silver shoes take just three steps, and each one is as fast as the wink of an eye.
The silver shoes take three steps, and then they stop so suddenly that Dorothy rolls over and over on the soft grass. At last she sits up and looks around her, and she cries out.
Just before her is the new farmhouse that Uncle Henry built after the cyclone carried the old one away. It is small and plain, but it is the most beautiful house that she has ever seen.

Uncle Henry is milking the cows, and Toto jumps out of her arms and runs barking toward the barn. Dorothy stands up in her stocking feet, because the silver shoes fell off in flight and are lost in the desert.
Aunt Em has just come out of the house to water the cabbages, when she looks up and sees Dorothy running toward her. She cries out, folds the little girl in her arms and covers her face with kisses.
Dorothy answers gravely that she has come from the Land of Oz, and she says that Toto is here too. Then she hugs Aunt Em tightly and says that she is so very glad to be home again.
C1C2: In the middle of the great Kansas prairie, where the land lay flat as a table in every direction, there lived a small girl named Dorothy. Her only playmate was a little black dog called Toto, who followed her wherever she went. Beyond the farm there was nothing to see but grass and sky, and a long road that nobody seemed to use.

The farmhouse was a very small one, for the wood to build it had to be hauled by wagon from many miles away. It held a rusty stove, a cupboard, a table, three or four chairs and two beds, all crowded into a single room. In the middle of the floor was a trap door that led to a little dark cellar, a hole dug for shelter when one of the great whirlwinds came.

The sun had burned the paint from the house and the wind had scoured the grass until everything had faded to the same dull gray. Aunt Em had come there as a young and pretty wife, yet she had lost the sparkle from her eyes, and Uncle Henry never laughed at all, working from morning till night. Only Toto kept the little girl from growing as gray as her surroundings, for his silky hair and merry black eyes were full of play.

One afternoon Uncle Henry sat at the door and looked anxiously at a sky that was grayer than ever before. From the north there came a low wailing of the wind, and as he listened he heard a shrill whistle from the south as well. He rose slowly to his feet, for he knew that something was gathering far beyond the edge of the prairie.

As the long grass bowed in waves before the rushing wind, Uncle Henry called to his wife that a cyclone was on its way. He ran at once to the sheds where the cows and horses were kept, for he could not bear to see them hurt. Aunt Em, who had been working at the stove, dropped her tasks and came to the door to see for herself.

One glance at the sky told Aunt Em how great the danger was, and she cried out to Dorothy to run for the cellar at once. She flung back the trap door in the floor and slipped down the ladder into the small, dark hole beneath. Her voice, sharp with fear, was the first time Dorothy had ever heard her sound so afraid.

Toto, frightened out of his wits, sprang from Dorothy's arms and fled under the big bed, where he crouched trembling in the farthest corner. Dorothy, who would not leave her dearest friend to face the storm alone, dragged him out and was starting for the trap door when the house gave a mighty shudder and she lost her footing. The boards groaned and the windows rattled as the wind tore at the roof, and she understood that it was far too late to reach the cellar.

Then something very strange happened, for the house whirled around two or three times and rose slowly through the air, as if it were a balloon. The north wind and the south wind met exactly where the house stood, and so it lay at the very center of the cyclone, where the air is usually quiet. Its great weight was carried upward higher and higher, until it was at the top of the whirling storm, and there it stayed.

It was very dark and the wind howled horribly around her, but Dorothy found that she was riding quite easily, since the house rocked her as a cradle might rock a baby. After the first few whirls and one terrible lurch, she felt as if she were being rocked gently, and she crawled upon her bed with Toto at her side. Though the house swayed and the wind wailed, the little girl soon closed her eyes and fell fast asleep.

She was awakened by a shock so sudden and so gentle that she would have been hurt if she had not been lying on the soft bed. For a moment she held her breath and wondered what had happened, while Toto put his cold little nose in her face and whined miserably. Then she noticed that the house was no longer moving, that the room was no longer dark, and that bright sunshine was streaming in at the window.

Dorothy sprang from her bed and, with Toto at her heels, ran to the door and flung it open. The little girl gave a cry of amazement as she looked about her, and her eyes grew bigger and bigger at the wonderful sights she saw. Nothing in all the gray years of her short life had prepared her for such a place.

The cyclone had set the house down very gently in the midst of a country of marvelous beauty, with stately trees bearing rich and luscious fruits. Banks of gorgeous flowers lined the paths, and birds with rare and brilliant plumage sang and fluttered in the branches. A little brook rushed and sparkled along between green banks, murmuring in a voice very grateful to a little girl who had lived so long on the dry, gray prairie.

While she stood looking eagerly at the strange and beautiful sights, she noticed a group of the queerest people she had ever seen coming toward her. They were not as big as the grown folk she was used to, but neither were they very small, for they seemed about as tall as Dorothy herself. The three men were dressed all in blue and wore round hats with little bells that tinkled sweetly as they moved.

The woman, who was very old, wore a pointed hat and a white gown spangled with little stars that glittered in the sun like diamonds. She bowed to Dorothy and said in a sweet voice that she was welcome to the land of the Munchkins. Then she thanked the girl warmly for killing the Wicked Witch of the East and for setting her people free from slavery.

Dorothy listened with wonder to this speech, for she could not imagine why the old woman called her a killer. She explained, very politely, that there must be some mistake, because she had never killed anything in all her life. It had been the cyclone that carried her here, and she had not done a single thing on purpose.

“Well, at any rate, your house did it,” answered the old woman with a little laugh, and she pointed to the corner of the house. Dorothy looked and gave a little cry of fright, for there, just under the corner of the great beam, two feet were sticking out, shod in silver shoes with pointed toes. The Wicked Witch of the East had been standing there when the house landed, and the weight of it had been the end of her.

The woman explained that the Wicked Witch had held all the Munchkins in bondage for many years, making them slave for her night and day. Now they were free at last, and they would be thankful to Dorothy for the rest of their lives. She herself was no Munchkin but the Witch of the North, a good witch who had always loved these small blue people.

Dorothy said that Aunt Em and Uncle Henry would be anxious about her, and she begged to be shown the way home to Kansas. The Witch of the North shook her head sadly and told her that Oz, with its four lands, was surrounded on all sides by a great desert, and that nobody could cross it alive. The little girl began to cry, since she was lonely among such strange people and it seemed that she would never go home.

There was one person, the old woman said, who might be able to help, and that was the Great Oz, who lived in the Emerald City at the center of the country. It was a long journey, and the way led along a road of yellow brick that Dorothy could not fail to follow. To protect the girl from harm on that journey, the old woman kissed her gently on the forehead and left a round, shining mark where her lips had touched.

The old woman handed over the silver shoes, saying that there was some charm connected with them but that she did not know what it was. Dorothy found that they fitted her as if they had been made for her, and she packed a loaf of bread in her basket with a white cloth. Then, with a friendly nod, the Witch of the North turned around on her left heel three times and vanished in a twinkling, and the Munchkins gave Dorothy a wondering look.

Left alone, Dorothy felt hungry, so she went to the cupboard and cut herself some bread, which she spread with butter. She gave a little to Toto, took a pail from the shelf and carried it to the brook, where she filled it with clear, sparkling water. Then she washed her face, put on her gingham dress and prepared to start her long journey to the Emerald City.

The road of yellow brick was not hard to find, for it lay just beyond her door, bright and clean and shining in the sun. As she walked, the silver shoes tinkled cheerfully on the hard yellow pavement, and Toto trotted beside her, wagging his tail and glancing up at his mistress. She had not felt so happy since the day the cyclone carried her away.

On both sides of the road were neat fences painted blue, and beyond them lay fields of grain and vegetables and the round houses of the Munchkins, which were all colored blue, since that was their favorite shade. The farmers and their wives stopped work to bow low as she went by, for everyone had heard that the strange little girl had destroyed the Wicked Witch and set them free. Dorothy, who had never been admired before, nodded back to them shyly and walked a little taller.

She walked for many miles that day, and toward evening her legs were so tired that she wondered where she should spend the night. At last she came to a house larger than the rest, and on the green lawn before it a crowd of people were dancing for joy. Five little fiddlers played as loudly as they could, and the laughing guests had set a great table loaded with fruits, nuts, pies and cakes.

The people greeted her kindly and invited her to supper and to stay the night, for it was the home of one of the richest Munchkins in the land, whose name was Boq. His friends had gathered to celebrate the end of the Wicked Witch, who had made them all slaves, and they were very glad to find the one who had freed them. Boq himself came to meet her, bowing politely and begging her to take a seat at his table.

Boq placed Dorothy in a seat near the head of the long table, and the kindly Munchkins brought her one delicious dish after another. She ate until she could eat no more, while Toto gnawed gratefully on a bone beneath her chair. All the time the little blue people watched her closely, admiring her silver shoes and whispering together about her wonderful journey.

Boq asked her where she was going, and Dorothy answered that she was on her way to the Emerald City to beg the Great Oz to send her back to Kansas. He looked at her thoughtfully and said that he did not know what the Wizard would do, but that he was very great and very mysterious. He added that he himself was a Munchkin who had never been near him, and that the journey was a long one.

When the feast was ended, Boq led her to a pleasant bedroom, where she found a bed with white sheets as smooth as snow. Dorothy sank into it with a sigh of happiness, and Toto curled himself up on the blue rug beside her, with his nose between his paws. In less than a minute they were both fast asleep, and not a single dream disturbed them until the morning.

The next morning she ate a hearty breakfast and watched a tiny Munchkin baby, who laughed and tugged at Toto's tail, as if he were the funniest thing in the world. Then she thanked Boq for all his goodness to her and started once more along the yellow road, in the clear bright light of the early day. The Emerald City was still many miles away, but Dorothy felt sure that she would reach it if she kept on walking.

Not far away from Boq's house, Dorothy came to a fine cornfield, and beside the road, on a tall pole, stood a figure made to scare the crows away. It wore a pointed blue hat, a blue jacket and a pair of old boots, and its face had been painted with two round eyes, a nose and a mouth. The head was a small sack stuffed with straw, and the whole thing stood so still that Dorothy felt quite certain it was staring at her.

To her astonishment, one of the painted eyes slowly winked at her, and Dorothy thought she must have been mistaken. Then the figure nodded its head in a friendly way, and she climbed over the fence and walked up to it while Toto ran around the pole, barking. The Scarecrow said good day in a rather husky voice and explained that it was very tedious to be perched up there night and day, scaring away crows.

Dorothy asked whether she could help him down, and the Scarecrow answered that the pole was stuck up his back and he could not move. She reached up with both hands, lifted the stuffed figure off the pole, and found that his body, being filled with straw, weighed hardly anything at all. He thanked her heartily for her kindness and then tumbled onto the soft grass at her feet, laughing as the loose straw tickled his nose.

Once on the ground, the Scarecrow bowed politely, stretched his arms and legs, and began to pat the straw back into shape wherever it had slipped. He declared that he felt like a new man, since being perched up there so long had made him stiff and sore. Then he asked who Dorothy was and where she was going, for he was a curious fellow and had seen so little of the world.

She told him that her name was Dorothy, that she was walking to the Emerald City, and that she hoped the Great Oz would send her back to Kansas. The Scarecrow looked blank and asked where the Emerald City might be, and who in the world Oz was. When she asked, with a smile, whether he really did not know, he sadly confessed that he knew nothing at all.

The Scarecrow confided that he had been made only two days earlier by a Munchkin farmer, who had painted his ears, eyes and nose. A young crow had at first flown away from him in fear, but an old crow had perched on his shoulder, laughed at his stuffed head, and then called all the other crows to eat the corn. If he had brains in his head, the old crow told him, he would be as good as any man, and brains were the only things worth having in this world.

He did not care at all about having a body of straw, said the Scarecrow, since it could not be hurt by a pin or a stumble, but he dreaded being thought a fool. Dorothy, whose heart was touched, said that if he would come with her she would beg the Wizard to do all he could for him. He thanked her with gratitude, and the odd pair, with Toto bounding alongside, climbed back over the fence to the road.

Toto sniffed suspiciously at the Scarecrow at first, as if he thought there might be a nest of rats in the straw, and growled at him unkindly. Before long the stuffed man stumbled where a brick was missing from the road and rolled on his face, yet he laughed so cheerfully at his clumsiness that the little dog soon changed his mind. Dorothy picked him up, helped him to his feet, and patted his straw into shape again.

As they walked, the Scarecrow said that he could not understand why Dorothy should wish to leave such a lovely country and go back to the dry, gray place she called Kansas. Dorothy answered that this was because he had no brains, and that people with real hearts and heads liked their own homes better than any other country, however beautiful it might be. He sighed and admitted that he could not know about such things, for his head was stuffed with straw.

That evening they came to a little cottage by the roadside, and since it was dark and Dorothy was tired, they decided to spend the night there. She gave Toto a crust, ate a little of her bread, and lay down on a bed of straw that the Scarecrow arranged for her, since he himself never grew weary. As she fell asleep, he stood patiently in a corner of the room and waited for the dawn.

At daybreak Dorothy washed her face in a clear little brook, ate a morsel of her bread, and was ready to travel once more. Before long they reached the edge of a forest so thick that the yellow road disappeared beneath the heavy branches overhead, and the shade made the day seem as dim as evening. The Scarecrow, who had no fear of anything except fire, led the way boldly into the gloom, while Dorothy and Toto followed close behind.

Deep in the forest the road ran between tall tree trunks, and the quiet was so heavy that every small sound seemed loud. Suddenly Dorothy heard a groan that was so sad it made her stop dead, and Toto answered with a little whine. The Scarecrow, who had no fear of anything but fire, said calmly that someone must be in trouble and they should go and see.

A few steps away, among the trees, they came upon a man made entirely of tin, with a funnel for a hat, standing as motionless as a statue. His axe was lifted over his head and rested against the trunk of a tree, as though he had been stopped in the middle of a blow. Dorothy stared in wonder, and the Scarecrow said nothing, while Toto barked sharply at the tin legs and hurt his teeth.

Dorothy asked whether it was he who had groaned, and the tin man answered, without moving his stiff jaws, that it was. He had been groaning for more than a year, he said, without anyone coming near. Only his eyes could turn toward them, and in a low voice he begged them to fetch an oil can from his little cottage, for his joints were rusted so tightly that he could not stir a muscle.

Dorothy hurried along a narrow path that led to the Woodman's little cottage, found the oil can on a shelf, and ran back to the road with it as fast as she could. She asked him where to begin, and he whispered that the neck was the worst, for he wanted to speak before anything else. So the Scarecrow held him steady while she squirted the oil carefully into the rusty joint.

She oiled his neck, and the Scarecrow bent his head gently from side to side until it moved freely, and the Tin Woodman was able to turn it himself. Next she oiled his jaws, then his arms and elbows and knees, and one by one the stiff joints squeaked and loosened. At last the Tin Woodman gave a sigh of relief, lowered his axe, and leaned it against the tree.

He thanked them fervently, declaring that but for their kindness he might have remained rooted there until the end of the world. They had rescued him from a dismal fate, he insisted, and he was curious to know what had brought two such travelers and a little dog into this lonely corner of the forest. The inquiry was so friendly that Dorothy told him at once about the yellow road and the Emerald City.

When Dorothy explained that they were bound for the Emerald City to see the Great Oz, the Tin Woodman thought for a moment and then asked whether Oz could give him a heart. He sat down on a log, and with a sigh he began to tell the story of how he had once been an ordinary man with a heart of his own. The Scarecrow and Dorothy listened closely, for it was a strange and sorrowful tale.

He had been born the son of a woodman, he said, and had grown up to chop down trees in the forest and to sell the wood. When his father died he cared for his old mother as long as she lived, and after she was gone he resolved to marry, so that he should not be lonely. He fell deeply in love with one of the beautiful Munchkin girls, who promised to marry him as soon as he could earn enough money to build a nicer house.

The girl lived with an old woman, who was so lazy that she did not want her helper to marry and leave her alone with all the cooking and cleaning. So she went to the Wicked Witch of the East and promised her two sheep and a cow if she would stop the wedding. The Witch cast a spell over the woodman's axe, so that next time he was chopping, it slipped and cut off his left leg.

At first the woodman thought this a great misfortune, since a man with one leg could never be a good chopper of trees. He went to a tinsmith, who made him a new leg out of tin, and when he had learned how to use it, he went joyfully back to his work. But the Wicked Witch was furious at this, for she had sworn that the girl would never marry him, and so she enchanted the axe again.

The Witch's spell did not stop there, and the axe slipped again and cut off his other leg, then both of his arms, and finally his head. Each time the tinsmith patiently made him a new part out of tin, so that the woodman went on working as bravely as ever. He told the story with such calm that it was hard to feel it had been a cruel one.

Finally the axe sliced through his body, and the tinsmith, after pondering a while, made a trunk of tin and joined it to his limbs with metal hinges. Now he was completely made of tin, and although he could work as before, he found that his heart was gone, and with it every feeling of love for the Munchkin girl. He no longer cared whether she married him or not, and he supposed that she was still waiting somewhere in the Munchkin land.

His body glittered in the sun, and he was proud of it, for now the axe could no longer hurt him. One day, however, he forgot to oil his joints, and a sudden rain fell on him while he was chopping and left him rooted to the spot. For a whole year he stood in the lonely forest and thought, and the saddest thing of all was knowing that he had lost his heart.

He told them that, if Oz would give him a heart, he would be as happy as any man in the world. The Scarecrow answered that he himself would rather have brains, for a fool would not know what to do with a heart if he had one. The Woodman replied firmly that a heart was by far the best thing, since brains do not make one happy, and happiness is the finest thing in the world.

Dorothy could not decide which of the two was right, but she felt sure that the Wizard could help them both if he chose. The Tin Woodman asked politely whether he might come too, and she gladly agreed, because the forest seemed less dark with a third friend. He fetched his axe and carried his oil can with him, and the four of them walked on together.

As they went along, the Tin Woodman accidentally stepped upon a beetle crossing the road and killed it, and the thought of this made him weep. The big tears ran down his face and rusted the hinges of his jaw, so that when Dorothy asked what was wrong, he could not open his mouth. She had to grab the oil can and set his jaw free, and he explained, with great earnestness, that one must watch one's steps, because a heart is a tender thing.

When night came, they made a camp under the thickest tree they could find, for there was no house near the road. Dorothy had only one small piece of bread left, so the Scarecrow gathered a basketful of nuts from a nearby tree and put them beside her to eat. The Tin Woodman chopped a pile of wood and made a bright fire, which the Scarecrow kept well away from, for he knew that a single spark would burn him up.

Late in the night a terrible roar shook the forest, and out of the black trees there bounded a great Lion, with his mane flying and his eyes shining in the firelight. With one blow of his paw he sent the Scarecrow spinning to the edge of the road, and the poor stuffed man lay there gasping for breath. Dorothy cried out, and Toto, who had been sleeping beside her, sprang up and began to bark at the huge animal.

Next the Lion struck at the Tin Woodman, who stood his ground and merely rang like a bell, while the claws of the beast scraped uselessly across the metal. The Lion drew back in some surprise, having never before met a creature that did not bleed, and in his confusion he caught sight of Toto, running toward him in a fury. The little dog was so brave that he did not stop to think, and the Lion opened his great mouth to bite him.

Fearing that Toto would be killed, Dorothy rushed forward without a moment's thought and slapped the Lion as hard as she could upon the nose. The huge beast stopped short, and then he sat down and rubbed his sore nose with his paw while tears welled up in his great round eyes. He was so astonished at being struck by such a small girl that he did not even try to defend himself.

“I didn't bite him,” said the Lion sadly, still rubbing his nose, and Dorothy answered that no, he had not, but he had certainly tried to. She told him that he was nothing but a big coward, and that it was shameful for such a great beast to strike a poor stuffed man who could not hurt a fly. The Lion hung his head and admitted, with a great sniff, that he had always known it and that it was the sorrow of his whole life.

The Lion, wiping a tear from his eye with the tip of his tail, said that he supposed he had been born that way. All the other animals expected him to be brave, for the lion is everywhere thought of as the King of Beasts, and he had learned that if he roared loudly every living thing ran from him. Whenever he met a man he was terribly afraid, but he only roared, and the man always fled as fast as he could go.

Whenever there was danger, said the Lion, his heart began to thump, and the Tin Woodman wondered aloud if the Lion might have a disease of the heart. If so, he continued, the Lion ought to be glad, since it proved that he had a heart, while he himself had none and so could not suffer from that sickness. The Lion thought about this very seriously and murmured that perhaps, if he had no heart, he would not be a coward at all.

He asked if he might go with them to the Emerald City and beg the Great Oz for a little courage, and the others agreed gladly, for he seemed a good-hearted beast. In the morning they came upon a deep ditch that cut across the road, with sides so steep that no one could climb them. The Lion looked at it carefully, measured the distance, and then carried each of them across on his back with a mighty spring, taking the Scarecrow first.

They went on through the forest, which grew darker and gloomier with every step, and soon they heard strange growls from deep among the trees. The Lion whispered that this was the part of the forest where the Kalidahs lived, savage beasts with the bodies of bears and the heads of tigers. Their claws were so long and sharp that they could tear him in two, and he confessed, shivering, that he was terribly afraid of them.

Presently they reached a second ditch, so wide and deep that even the Lion shook his head and said that he could never leap across it. The friends sat down on the edge to think, and the Scarecrow, studying a great tree that grew near the brink, suggested that the Tin Woodman might chop it down so that it fell across the gap. The Lion remarked that this was a clever thought, and that it almost sounded as if the Scarecrow had brains in his head.

The Tin Woodman set to work at once, and his axe was so sharp that before long the tree was nearly cut through. The Lion put his strong shoulder to the trunk and pushed with all his might, and the tree tottered, swayed and fell with a great crash across the ditch, its top branches resting on the opposite side. They stood admiring the strange bridge, and the Scarecrow said that it was a fine thing to have a friend who could think of such a way.

They had begun to cross, with the Scarecrow in front and Dorothy holding Toto close, when a fierce growl made them look back toward the forest. Two terrible Kalidahs, with their long teeth shining and their paws pounding the earth, were bounding toward them at a great speed. The Lion, who was trembling in every limb, cried out that they were lost, but the Scarecrow urged him to follow Dorothy across the bridge.

The Lion, whose heart was beating terribly, took one look back and bounded over the tree with a single enormous leap, and the Kalidahs sprang onto the trunk after him. The Scarecrow shouted to the Tin Woodman to chop the bridge in half, and the Woodman, who never missed a stroke, struck the trunk so hard that it split and fell. With a howl of rage the two snarling monsters tumbled into the ditch, and the friends heard nothing more of them.

Soon the friends reached the edge of the forest, and Dorothy gave a great sigh of relief as she stepped out into the sunshine. Before them rolled a broad river, rushing swiftly between its banks, and on the far side they could see the yellow bricks of the road glittering in the light. The Tin Woodman chopped down some trees and fastened the logs together with willow branches, and by evening there was a strong raft ready to float them over.

The Scarecrow took the long pole and pushed against the bottom of the river, but the current was so swift that it swept the raft far away from the yellow road. Suddenly the end of the pole stuck fast in the mud, and before the Scarecrow could pull it free, the raft sailed on and left him clinging to the pole in the middle of the stream. The others cried out in dismay, and the poor Scarecrow remarked that he was now worse off than when he met Dorothy.

As the raft drifted down the river, the Lion leaped into the water and swam hard, towing them behind him with the Tin Woodman holding firmly to his tail. It was a heavy task, but he was strong, and Dorothy took the pole and pushed as well. When at last they stepped out upon the bank, the little girl was weak and tired, but she was very glad to stand on solid ground.

As they walked along the river bank they heard a call, and a long-legged Stork came flying toward the Scarecrow, who was still hanging on his pole. The bird asked who he was and what he was doing, and when the Scarecrow explained that he was only stuffed with straw, the Stork laughed and said that he would not be hard to carry. He seized the pole in his claws, lifted the Scarecrow high into the air and carried him to the green bank where his friends were waiting.

Presently they came to a meadow where the grass was bright with flowers, and further on lay a vast field of red poppies, more beautiful than any Dorothy had ever seen. The scent was so sweet and strong that she wanted to walk into it and pick the biggest ones, and she smiled at the sunshine and the bees. She did not know that the smell of poppies is so powerful that anyone who breathes it long enough falls asleep, and if not carried away, sleeps forever.

Before long Dorothy's eyes grew heavy, and she felt that she must rest her head among the flowers, just for a moment. The Tin Woodman urged her to run, but it was too late, and she sank down among the red petals, where her little dog soon dropped beside her and the great Lion lay down with a yawn. The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman were not troubled, for neither had any flesh to be put to sleep.

The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, who were not made of flesh and blood, took Dorothy and Toto in their arms and hurried away out of the field of deadly flowers. They found a pleasant spot on the soft grass beside a stream, far from the poppies, and laid the girl there to breathe the fresh air and wake up by herself. Then they looked back at the great sleeping Lion, so heavy that no one could ever lift him.

While they stood wondering what to do, they heard a low growl, and a great yellow wildcat came racing across the meadow after a tiny field mouse. The Tin Woodman, who did not believe in letting a helpless creature be harmed, swung his axe so close to the wildcat's head that it turned and fled. The mouse, quivering with fear, said in a squeaking voice that the Woodman had saved her life.

She was, as it turned out, the Queen of all the Field Mice, and she bowed graciously before the Tin Woodman, who had no heart but behaved with a great deal of kindness. She offered to do anything that her people could do in return for such a gift, and the Scarecrow, whose brain was working quickly, asked whether the mice could help them to save their large friend. The Queen listened to the story of the sleeping Lion and agreed to call her subjects at once.

The Queen blew a whistle, and in a few minutes thousands of mice came running from every direction. The Tin Woodman made a small, strong truck from logs, and the Scarecrow and he rolled the sleeping Lion onto it, while each mouse tied a string to the truck and took the other end in its teeth. In this way the great beast was drawn away from the dangerous flowers, as swiftly as a feather on a breeze, though the Lion was much heavier than all the mice together.

The Lion woke up at last on the soft grass, yawned, stretched himself and expressed great pleasure at being alive, for he had never smelled such a deadly flower. The Queen and her mice scampered back to their fields after many thanks from the grateful travelers, and before she left she promised that she would come at once if any of them ever needed her help. By then Dorothy was awake too, and she looked around with a smile and said that they should be going.

The yellow road led them over smoother ground, and the farther they went the greener the country became, until the fences and the houses beside the road were painted green. The people they passed were dressed in green from head to foot, and they all stared at the strange company of a girl, a lion, a scarecrow and a man of tin. Dorothy noticed that nobody came near them, as though everyone were a little afraid of the great Lion.

They had to sleep beside the road that night, for they found no house that would take them in, and the Tin Woodman made a bed of leaves under a tall tree. Before she closed her eyes, Dorothy looked up and noticed that the sky in front of them glowed with a faint and shimmering green, as if a lamp were burning behind the hills. It was a wonderful sight, and she fell asleep wondering what could cause such light.

In the morning they walked on until they came to a high, thick wall that sparkled green in the sunlight, with a great gate set in the center. The gate was studded with emeralds that glittered so brightly that even the Scarecrow's painted eyes were dazzled. Beside it hung a bell, and Dorothy pulled the cord, which sounded with a silver note.

The gate swung open slowly, and a small man in a green coat stepped out and asked what they wished in the Emerald City. When Dorothy answered that they had come to see the Great Oz, he looked amazed, and warned them that the Wizard was powerful and terrible, and could destroy them if they came on a foolish errand. Dorothy replied that theirs was not a foolish errand, and that they had heard Oz was a good Wizard.

The Guardian answered that Oz was indeed good and ruled the city wisely, though he was terrible to those who came out of curiosity or dishonesty. Before they entered, he said, they must put on spectacles, since otherwise the brightness and glory of the Emerald City would blind them. Even the people who lived there, he added, wore spectacles night and day, for Oz had ordered it when the city was first built.

The Guardian opened a large box that was full of spectacles of every size and shape, all with green glass in them, and fitted a pair to each of the travelers, including the Lion and Toto. He fastened them with a golden band that went around the back of the head, and locked it with a tiny key that hung on a chain about his neck. Then he put on a pair himself, and they were ready to enter the city.

Through the gate lay streets lined with houses built of green marble and studded everywhere with glittering emeralds, and the sun seemed to pour green light over everything. The pavement was of the same green marble, and the joints between the blocks were set with rows of emeralds that sparkled in the sunshine. Dorothy gazed about her with her mouth open, and even the Lion looked as if he were dreaming.

Everywhere there were people in green clothes, and every shop seemed to be selling green wares, for there were green candy and green popcorn, green shoes and hats of every size. A man was selling green lemonade at the corner, and the little children who bought it carried it away in green cups. The people looked happy and well fed, although there were no horses in the street, only men pushing carts of green goods.

At last they came to the great palace, where a soldier with a long green beard stood guarding the door. The Guardian explained that the strangers wished to see the Great Oz, and the soldier asked them to wait in a small hall while he carried the message to the Wizard. He warned them that the Wizard was not likely to see them at once, or even that day.

After a long wait the soldier returned and said that Oz would receive them in the morning, one at a time, and a green girl led Dorothy to a pretty bedroom. There she laid out a gown of green silk and tied a green ribbon around Toto's neck, while the others were shown to rooms of their own. Dorothy fell asleep that night on a soft bed in the heart of the Emerald City, half expecting to wake up in Kansas.

In the morning the green maid brought Dorothy to the great Throne Room, where an emerald throne stood in the center, under a high green dome. Upon the throne sat an enormous head, bigger than the head of the biggest giant, with no body to support it and no arms or legs. Dorothy looked at it with wonder and fear, and the eyes turned slowly and gazed at her sharply and steadily.

A great voice, which seemed to come from the head, said that it was Oz, the Great and Terrible, and asked who she was and why she had come. Dorothy answered that she was Dorothy, small and meek, and that she had come for help. The eyes looked at her silver shoes and at the mark on her forehead, and the voice asked where she had got them.

She told him how the house had fallen on the Witch of the East, and then she asked to be sent back to Kansas. The head answered that she must do something for him first, and that she must kill the Wicked Witch of the West, since she had destroyed the other and wore the magic shoes. Dorothy burst into tears, for she had never willingly killed anything, and she did not know how she could begin.

The next day the Scarecrow entered the Throne Room expecting the Head, but instead he found a lovely lady sitting on the throne, with a crown of jewels on her green hair. Wings of gorgeous color grew from her shoulders, so light that they stirred at the slightest breath of air. The Scarecrow bowed politely and begged her to put brains into his head instead of straw.

On the third day the Tin Woodman met a terrible Beast, as big as an elephant, with the head of a rhinoceros, five eyes, five arms and five long, thin legs. The Woodman, who had no heart to be afraid with, stood calmly before it and asked for a heart so that he might be like other men. The Beast replied that he would first have to destroy the Wicked Witch of the West.

On the fourth day the Cowardly Lion walked into the Throne Room and found only a ball of fire, so fierce and glowing that he could hardly bear to look at it. He trembled and begged the Wizard to give him courage, so that in truth he might be King of the Beasts, as men called him. The voice answered that he must bring proof that the Witch was dead, and until then he must remain a coward.

That evening the four friends sat in Dorothy's room and told one another what they had seen, and they were astonished to find that no two of them had met the same Oz. Dorothy had seen a head, the Scarecrow a lovely lady, the Woodman a beast and the Lion a ball of fire. Yet all had been given the same terrible task, and not one of them knew how to carry it out.

Dorothy said that she supposed she would have to try, for she wanted to go home above everything, and the Scarecrow declared that he would go with her, though he thought he would not be much use. The Tin Woodman added that he would do anything for a heart, and the Lion confessed that he would go even if he were frightened to death. So it was settled, and the friends retired early to their beds, resolved to depart at first light and to trust their fortune to the road.

In the morning the soldier led them to the Guardian of the Gates, who unlocked their spectacles and put them back into the great green box, and they all asked him which road they should take. There was no road, he told them, for nobody ever wished to go to the West, and the Witch would surely find them as soon as they entered her country. He advised them to keep to the west, where the sun sets, and then they could not fail to find her.

They said farewell and started toward the west over fields of soft grass sprinkled with daisies and buttercups. Dorothy was still wearing the pretty silk dress that she had put on in the palace, but to her surprise it was no longer green, for it had turned pure white, and so had the ribbon around Toto's neck. As the Emerald City dropped behind, the ground grew rougher and hillier, and they saw no farms or houses.

The Wicked Witch of the West had but one eye, yet it was as powerful as a telescope and could see everywhere. As she sat in the door of her castle one day, she happened to glance around and saw Dorothy asleep with her friends all about her, a long way off. She was angry to find them in her country, so she blew upon a silver whistle that hung around her neck.

From all directions there came running to her a pack of wolves, with long legs, fierce eyes and sharp teeth. The Witch ordered them to go to the travelers and tear them to pieces, adding that she did not wish to make them slaves, since one was made of tin and one of straw and none was fit to work. The leader of the pack dashed away at full speed, and all the other wolves followed him.

Luckily the Scarecrow and the Woodman were awake and heard the wolves coming, so that the Woodman could seize his axe and stand ready. He asked the Scarecrow to stay behind him, and as each wolf came near, he swung his arm and the animal fell dead at his feet. There were forty wolves, and forty times the axe swung, until at last they all lay in one heap before him.

She saw all her wolves lying dead, and the strangers still traveling through her country, which made her angrier than before, so she blew her silver whistle twice. A great flock of wild crows came flying toward her, so many that they darkened the sky, and she ordered them to fly to the strangers and peck out their eyes. The crows wheeled around in a great black circle and set off across the sky, croaking harshly as they went toward the travelers.

The Scarecrow said that this was his battle, and he told the others to lie down beside him and not to be harmed. When the crows saw him, they were frightened at first, but the King Crow remarked that it was only a stuffed man and flew at him with a croak. The Scarecrow caught each bird by the neck as it came, and forty times he twisted, until all were lying dead beside him.

In a fury the Witch called for her black bees, and she told them to fly to the strangers and sting them to death. The bees were a great swarm, buzzing and humming, and they flew straight toward the travelers with their stings pointed forward. The Woodman, who saw them coming, understood that Dorothy and the Lion would be the only ones in real danger.

The Woodman told the Scarecrow to take his straw and scatter it over Dorothy, Toto and the Lion, so that the bees could not find them. The bees came, found nobody to sting except the Tin Woodman, and broke their stingers against his tin without hurting him at all. Since bees cannot live without their stingers, that was the end of the black swarm, and they lay scattered around him like little heaps of fine coal.

Dorothy and the Lion got up, and with the Woodman's help they stuffed the straw back into the Scarecrow until he was as good as ever, and the party continued their journey. The Wicked Witch, who had seen all this, was so angry that she sent a band of her Winkie slaves to bring the strangers back. They carried spears, and she told them to be sure to do her bidding, but the Lion gave a great roar and sent them all fleeing in terror.

Then the Witch took from her cupboard a Golden Cap, set round with diamonds and rubies, which gave its owner the power to call the Winged Monkeys. They would obey three commands from the one who wore it, and she had used this power twice already, once to make the Winkies her slaves and once to drive the Great Oz from her land. She now had only one command left, and she decided that the time had come to use it.

She put on the cap, stood on her left foot and said slowly the magic words, and in a moment the air was filled with the noise of flapping wings. The King of the Winged Monkeys bowed low and asked what she commanded for this third and last time. The Witch told him to destroy the strangers who had dared to enter her land, except for the Lion, whom she wished to harness and make work like a horse.

The Monkeys swooped down on the travelers, and some of them seized the Tin Woodman and bore him high over a country strewn with sharp rocks. There they let him fall, and he lay far below, so dented and battered that he could neither move nor groan. Others caught the Scarecrow, pulled every wisp of straw from his clothes and head, and hurled the bundle of hat, boots and coat into the top branches of a tall tree.

The rest of the band threw thick coils of rope around the Lion, around his body, his head and his legs, until he could neither bite nor claw. Then they lifted him into the air and carried him, roaring helplessly, to the Witch's castle. He was set down in a small yard surrounded by a high iron fence, so that he could never escape.

But when the Monkeys came to Dorothy, their leader saw the mark of the Good Witch's kiss on her forehead and stopped short. He told the others that they dared not harm the little girl, for she was protected by the Power of Good, which is greater than the Power of Evil. All they could do was to carry her gently to the castle of the Wicked Witch and leave her there, with Toto in her arms.

The Witch was both surprised and alarmed when she saw the mark on Dorothy's forehead, and when she looked at the silver shoes she began to shake with fear. She was tempted at first to run away, but she looked into the child's eyes and saw how simple the soul behind them was, and that the girl had no idea of the wonderful power of her shoes. The Witch laughed to herself and thought that she could still make Dorothy her slave.

The Witch led her through many rooms of the castle to the kitchen, where she was ordered to clean the pots and kettles, sweep the floor and keep the fire fed with wood. Dorothy went to work meekly, for she decided to do her best and hoped that the Witch would not kill her. While she toiled, Toto sat beside her and the old woman left to harness the Lion like a horse.

The Witch went out to the Lion's yard, thinking it would be amusing to harness him like a horse, but when she opened the gate he gave such a roar that she fled in fear. She locked the gate and shouted that he should have nothing to eat until he did as she wished. Every night, while the Witch slept, Dorothy crept out with food, and the Lion ate it gratefully and told her how much he longed to be free.

The Witch wanted the Silver Shoes more than anything, but she was afraid of the dark and of water, and so dared not take them off Dorothy's feet at night or while she was washing. She placed an iron bar in the middle of the kitchen floor and made it invisible by her magic, so that when Dorothy walked across it she stumbled and fell. One of her silver shoes flew off, and before she could reach it, the Witch had snatched it away and put it on her own thin foot.

Dorothy cried that the Witch was a wicked creature and had no right to take her shoe, but the Witch replied that she would keep it and would get the other one too. This made Dorothy so angry that she snatched up the bucket of water that stood nearby and dashed it over the old woman, wetting her from head to foot. Instantly the wicked woman gave a loud cry of fear, and the girl looked at her in wonder as something strange began to happen.

As Dorothy stared, the Witch began to shrink and fall away, and she wailed that in a few minutes she would melt entirely. She asked in a despairing voice whether the child had not known that water would be the end of her, and Dorothy answered truthfully that she had not. The Witch declared that she had been wicked in her day, but never dreamed that a little girl could melt her, and with those words she fell down in a brown, shapeless mass.

Seeing that the Witch had really melted away to nothing, Dorothy drew another bucket of water and threw it over the mess, and then she swept it all out of the door. The only thing left was the silver shoe, which she picked out, cleaned and dried with a cloth and put on her foot again. Then, being free at last to do as she chose, she ran out to the courtyard to tell the Lion the happy news.

Dorothy ran to the courtyard, unfastened the gate and told the Lion that the Wicked Witch of the West had come to an end. The great beast was so delighted that he wept like a child, and Dorothy used the corner of her apron to dry the tears from his mane. They were no longer prisoners, she said, and they were no longer in a strange land where they were not welcome.

The yellow Winkies, who had been the Witch's slaves for many long years, came out into the yard and cheered when they heard the news. They bowed to Dorothy and to the Lion, and they said that they would never forget the little girl who had set them free. That night they held a feast in the Witch's castle, and for the first time in their lives they laughed aloud.

Dorothy asked them whether they would help her find her friends, and the Winkies answered that they would do anything for her. They set out with the Lion and walked for a day and a night, until they found the Tin Woodman lying among the sharp rocks, bent and dented and covered with scratches. The Winkies lifted him gently, carried him back to the castle, and Dorothy wept a few tears over her old friend.

Dorothy asked whether any of the Winkies were tinsmiths, and a number of them stepped forward, saying that they could mend the Woodman as good as new. They worked on him for three days and four nights, hammering, twisting, bending and soldering his legs and arms and body. When they had finished, he was almost as good as he had been before, except that his body was covered with patches.

The Tin Woodman walked about the room, still a little stiff, and then he thanked the Winkies for their skill with a bow so graceful that it made them smile. Tears of joy ran down his face when he saw Dorothy again, and she dried them carefully with her apron, while she oiled his joints to prevent them from rusting. He said that he was happier than he had ever been, and he declared that he would not rest until the Scarecrow was found.

Next they went in search of the Scarecrow, and the Winkies led them in every direction until at last they found the tall tree where his clothes still hung among the branches. It was so tall and the trunk so smooth that no one could climb it, and Dorothy looked up at the bundle with great sadness. The Tin Woodman, however, said at once that he would chop it down, for the Scarecrow needed his clothes.

The Tin Woodman, who had been busy chopping for a while, swung his axe with such strength that in a few minutes the tree began to totter. It fell with a crash, and the Scarecrow's hat, boots, coat and shirt tumbled out of the branches and lay on the ground. The Winkies gathered them up and carried them back to the castle, while the Lion trotted behind, looking proud and relieved.

At the castle the kind Winkies stuffed the Scarecrow's coat and trousers with fine fresh straw, so that he stood up bright and plump, as good as new. The Scarecrow thanked them over and over again, and he thanked Dorothy most of all, since without her friendship he might have stayed in the tree forever. The four friends then spent several happy days at the castle, where everything they wanted was given to them.

The Winkies were so fond of the Tin Woodman that they begged him to stay and rule over them, now that the Wicked Witch was gone. He answered, with a kindness that touched them, that he would gladly do so one day, but that he must first return to the Emerald City and claim the heart that Oz had promised. They gave gifts to all of them, and the Winkies, who had no use for gold, pressed jewels and fine things upon each traveler.

Before they left, Dorothy found the Golden Cap in the Witch's cupboard, with its band of diamonds and rubies, and tried it on her head. It fitted her perfectly, and since she knew nothing of its magic, she merely thought it was pretty and wore it. Then she waved goodbye to the Winkies, and the four friends set off toward the east, to claim the promises of the Great Oz.

The friends walked toward the east, where the sun rose each morning, but they soon found that there was no road in that wild country, only high grass, rocks and hills. All day they wandered here and there with the sun in their eyes, until they realized that they could not tell where the yellow road had gone. When night came, they sat down in the grass, hungry and weary and very much discouraged.

Dorothy suddenly remembered the cap she wore, and since she had read the words written on it, she resolved to try its magic and see what would happen. She stood on one foot, recited the strange charm slowly and clearly, and in a few seconds the air was full of the noise of wings. The King of the Winged Monkeys bowed low before her and asked what she wished them to do.

She told the King that she wished to be carried to the Emerald City before nightfall, and he replied that it would be done at once. The Monkeys obeyed whoever held the Golden Cap, he said, but they could never leave the Land of Oz, for they belonged to this country alone. Then the wild creatures picked up Dorothy and her friends in their strong arms and flew away through the sky.

As they flew, the Monkey King told her that his people had once lived freely in a great forest, flying from tree to tree and eating nuts, and bowing to no master. His grandfather had been their king in those days, and he loved a joke better than a good dinner. Then he told the tale of the princess Gayelette, who made the Golden Cap, and of how his people came to serve it.

The princess Gayelette, who ruled in the North, was about to marry a fine young man named Quelala, when the Monkey King's grandfather and his band seized him and dropped him in a river for a joke. The young man swam to shore, laughing, but his rich silks and velvets were ruined, and the princess was very angry. She forgave the Monkeys only on one condition: that they should do the bidding of the owner of the Golden Cap three times.

In a short while the Monkeys set the four friends gently down before the gate of the Emerald City and flew back into the sky with many bows to Dorothy. The Guardian opened the gate in great surprise at seeing them again, and when he heard that the Wicked Witch had been melted, he exclaimed that it was marvelous news. He fastened their spectacles on again, and he led them to the palace, bowing to Dorothy most of the way.

The soldier carried their message to Oz, and the Wizard sent back the reply that they might wait, but that he would see nobody that day. The same thing happened the next day, and the next, and for four whole days the friends sat idle in their green rooms, while the Scarecrow and the Lion grumbled about promises that were not kept. Dorothy grew sadder and sadder, and the Tin Woodman threatened to break down a door if he had to.

At last, on the fifth day, the soldier announced that the Great Oz would see them in the Throne Room, and they hurried there without a moment's delay. The great hall was empty, except for a screen in the corner and a deep, booming voice that came from somewhere above the throne. It asked them what they wished, and Dorothy answered that they had come to claim the promises Oz had made.

The voice demanded whether the Witch was really dead, and when Dorothy said that she had melted her with a pail of water, it replied that they must come back tomorrow, since it needed time to think. The Lion decided that it might be good to frighten the Wizard, and he let out a mighty roar that made Toto jump back in alarm. The little dog knocked over the screen in the corner, and behind it stood a bald, wrinkled old man who looked as astonished as they were.

The Tin Woodman raised his axe and rushed at the little man, asking him who he was, and the old man answered in a trembling voice that he was Oz, the Great and Terrible. He begged them not to strike him, and he promised to do anything they wanted if they would spare him. The friends stared in dismay, for each of them had pictured a very different Oz, and not one of them had expected a meek, bald old man.

“I thought Oz was a great Head,” said Dorothy, and the others each told what they had seen, a lovely lady, a beast and a ball of fire. The little man replied meekly that they were all wrong, for he had only been making believe, and he begged them to speak softly lest someone overhear. He was supposed to be a Great Wizard, he admitted, but in truth he was just a common man, and, as the Scarecrow said sadly, a humbug.

Oz led them into a small chamber behind the Throne Room, where the great Head lay in a corner, made of many thicknesses of paper with a carefully painted face. He explained that he hung it from the ceiling by a wire, stood behind the screen and moved the eyes and mouth by pulling a thread, while throwing his voice like a ventriloquist. He also showed them the mask and dress of the lovely lady, the beast made of sewn skins and a ball of cotton that burned fiercely when oil was poured on it.

He had been born in Omaha, said Oz, and when Dorothy cried out that this was not far from Kansas, he sadly replied that it was a good deal farther from here. As a young man he had learned to throw his voice like any ventriloquist, and later he became a balloonist who rose on circus days to draw a crowd. Dorothy listened carefully, because she was beginning to understand how a man might arrive in the clouds.

One day the ropes got twisted, and the balloon went up above the clouds, so far that a current of air caught it and carried it for many miles. For a day and a night he traveled through the air, and on the morning of the second day he awoke and found the balloon floating over a strange and beautiful country. It came down gradually, he went on, and he was not hurt a bit, but he found himself among people who stared at him with astonishment.

Seeing him come from the clouds, the people thought he must be a great Wizard, and he naturally let them think so, since they were afraid of him and promised to do whatever he asked. Merely to amuse himself and keep the good people busy, he ordered them to build the city and his palace, which they did willingly and well. Then, because the land was so green and lovely, he named it the Emerald City, and to make the name fit better he made all the people wear green spectacles.

He had shut himself up in the palace, said Oz, because one of his greatest fears was the Witches, for while he had no magic at all, they could do wonderful things. The Witches of the North and South were good, but those of the East and West were terribly wicked, and he had lived in dread of them for years. He had promised Dorothy anything if she would destroy the Witch of the West, and now, he said, he was ashamed that he could not keep his word.

“I think you are a very bad man,” said Dorothy, and the little man answered, with a smile, that he was really a very good man, though he had to admit that he was a very bad Wizard. When the Scarecrow asked for brains, Oz told him that he did not need them, for he was learning something every day, and experience was the only thing that brought knowledge. The Scarecrow insisted that he would still be unhappy until he had some, and Oz sighed and agreed to try.

The Lion, who was anxious, asked about his courage, and Oz answered that all he needed was confidence in himself, since every living thing is afraid when it faces danger. True courage, he said, is facing danger when you are afraid, yet the Lion replied that he would still be unhappy until he had the kind that makes one forget his fear. The Tin Woodman added that he would bear any sorrow for a heart, and Oz promised both of them what they wanted the next day.

The next morning the Scarecrow came to the Throne Room, and Oz took off his head and emptied out the straw. Then he went into a back room and mixed a measure of bran with a number of pins and needles. He shook the mixture well, filled the top of the head with it and stuffed the rest with straw before fastening the head back on, and the Scarecrow declared that he felt wise indeed.

For the Woodman, Oz cut a small square hole in the left side of his chest with a pair of tinsmith's shears, took out a pretty heart made of silk and stuffed with sawdust, and fitted it neatly in place. He covered the hole with a square patch, saying that he was sorry about it, and the Woodman declared that he was far too happy to care. Then Oz poured a green liquid from a bottle into a dish for the Lion and told him to drink it, and the Lion, who now felt full of courage, said that it was exactly what he had wanted.

The Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Lion were delighted with their new gifts and walked about the palace in great spirits, but Dorothy could not share their joy. For three days she heard nothing from Oz, and as she sat by the window looking out at the green towers, she thought sadly of Aunt Em and Uncle Henry and the gray farm in Kansas. Even Toto could not make her smile, and she wondered whether she would ever see her home again.

On the fourth day Oz sent for her, and he told her cheerfully that he believed he had found a way out of the country. He had come to Oz in a balloon, and she had come through the air in a cyclone, so he reasoned that the surest passage over the desert lay through the air. Since a cyclone was beyond his powers, he explained, he would build a balloon instead, and Dorothy asked eagerly how such a marvel could be accomplished.

A balloon, Oz explained, was made of silk coated with glue to keep the gas in, and he had plenty of silk in the palace, but there was no gas in the whole country to fill it. The only other way to make it float was with hot air, which was not so good, for if it grew cold the balloon would come down in the desert. He added that he was tired of being a humbug, and that he would rather go back to Kansas with Dorothy and join a circus again.

Dorothy took a needle and thread, and as quickly as Oz cut the strips of silk into proper shape she stitched them neatly together, first a strip of light green, then one of dark green and then one of emerald. It took three days to sew all the strips together, but when it was finished they had a big bag of green silk more than twenty feet long. Oz painted it on the inside with a coat of thin glue to make it airtight, and then he announced that the balloon was ready.

A basket was needed for them to ride in, so Oz sent the soldier with the green whiskers to fetch a big clothes basket, which he fastened to the bottom of the balloon with many ropes. When all was ready, he sent word to his people that he was going to pay a visit to a great brother Wizard who lived in the clouds. The news spread rapidly through the city, and everyone hurried to see the wonderful sight.

Oz ordered the balloon to be carried out in front of the Palace, and the people gazed upon it with the greatest curiosity. The Tin Woodman had chopped a big pile of wood, and now he kindled a roaring fire. Oz held the mouth of the balloon over the flames so that the rising hot air would be caught in the silken bag, and gradually it swelled out and lifted until the basket just touched the ground.

Oz stepped into the basket and told the people in a loud voice that he was now going away to make a visit, and that while he was gone the Scarecrow would rule over them. He commanded them to obey the Scarecrow as faithfully as they had ever obeyed him, and to be kind to the strangers. By this time the balloon was tugging hard at the rope that held it to the ground, for the air inside it was hot, and this made it much lighter than the air without.

“Come, Dorothy,” called the Wizard, but she answered that she could not find Toto, because she did not wish to leave her dear little dog behind. Toto had run into the crowd to bark at a kitten, and Dorothy at last found him, picked him up and ran toward the balloon. She was within a few steps of it, and Oz was holding out his hands to help her into the basket.

Just then, crack went the ropes, and the balloon rose into the air without her. Dorothy screamed to the Wizard to come back, for she wanted to go too, but he called down that he could not come back, since the balloon was climbing higher every moment. He bade her goodbye, and the crowd shouted goodbye, all eyes turned upward to the Wizard riding in his basket.

That was the last that any of them ever saw of Oz, the Wonderful Wizard, although he may have reached Omaha safely, and be there now, for all they knew. The people remembered him lovingly, and said to one another that Oz was always their friend, who had built them the beautiful Emerald City and now had left the Wise Scarecrow to rule over them. Still, for many days they grieved over his loss and would not be comforted.

Dorothy wept bitterly over the loss of the balloon, which had been her only hope of returning to Kansas. Her friends gathered around her and tried to comfort her, and the Tin Woodman, who knew that he must not cry in case his joints rusted, patted her hand gently. The Scarecrow, who now ruled the city, declared that it was not wise to give up while there was still a chance of finding another way.

At last the soldier with the green whiskers suggested that they ask Glinda, the Good Witch of the South, who was the most powerful of all the Witches. She ruled over the Quadlings, and her castle stood on the edge of the desert, so she might know a way to cross it. The soldier warned them that the road to the south was full of dangers, with dark forests and fierce beasts and strange people.

Dorothy resolved at once to seek Glinda, and the Lion declared that he would go with her even if his knees shook, while the Woodman and the Scarecrow said that they would not leave her. The next morning Dorothy kissed the soldier with the green whiskers goodbye and shook hands warmly with the Guardian of the Gates. Then the friends passed out through the gate and set off, with Toto at her heels, toward the south.

For a day they walked through pleasant country, with soft grass and gay flowers, and rich fruit hanging within reach of Dorothy's hand. Toward evening they came to a great forest, whose trees were so large and so close together that the branches met overhead. The yellow road did not run there, and there seemed to be no way around the forest, and none to the left or the right.

The Scarecrow walked up to the nearest tree to look for a gap between its branches, but the huge branches bent down at once and twined around him. The tree lifted him up and hurled him headlong among his friends, and the Scarecrow gave a cry of surprise, though he was not hurt at all. Dorothy helped him to his feet and reflected, with a shiver, that these must be trees that fight, and that their way would not be easy.

The Tin Woodman raised his axe and marched to the next tree, and when its great branch bent down to seize him, he chopped it in two with a single blow. At once the tree began to shake as if in pain, and the Tin Woodman slipped under it and passed safely through the forest. The others followed him one by one, and the rest of the trees did not stir.

Beyond the Fighting Trees the road came out upon a high wall, which was as smooth and white as the surface of a dish and much higher than their heads. There seemed to be no door or gate in it, and the Scarecrow, who had begun to value his new brains, said that they must find a way to climb over. The wall was made of china, as the Tin Woodman discovered when he tapped it with his knuckle.

While the others rested, the Tin Woodman returned to the forest, and with his axe he cut down one of the smaller trees, split it, and began to make a strong ladder. It took him the whole afternoon, since he was careful about each rung, but when it was done, it rose against the wall as straight as a mast. Dorothy thanked him, and the Scarecrow said that no one could have made a better one.

The Scarecrow climbed first, and when he reached the top of the wall and looked over, he cried out in astonishment. Dorothy followed him, and she, too, cried “Oh my” when she saw the strange land below, and the Tin Woodman and the Lion climbed up beside them.
