Beneath them lay a country as smooth and white as the bottom of a big dish, with little houses and animals that seemed to be made of china.

Everything in that land was made of china, from the houses and fences to the cows, the sheep and the little men and women, and all of it was brightly painted and not much higher than Dorothy's knee. The friends stepped carefully over the white floor, for a startled china cow had just kicked over a milkmaid's pail and broken her own leg, and the china folk warned them that anything broken could never be quite mended. A lovely Princess, with a china clown, begged them politely to be careful and to go away soon.

The friends were glad to leave the little china land before they did more harm, and as they went the Lion's tail swung round and knocked over a china church, which crashed to pieces. Dorothy remarked that they had been lucky to break so little, and she hoped that the china people would forgive them. They climbed back down the wall, where the great forest lay waiting on the other side.

The forest they came to next was thick and dark, and it was full of wild beasts of every kind. The Lion, who had a sharp ear, heard a great growling in the distance, and when he led his friends forward, they found a large open place under the trees where hundreds of animals were gathered. There were tigers, elephants, bears, wolves and foxes, and they all looked anxious and troubled.

A great tiger bowed before the Lion and greeted him as the King of Beasts, saying that he had come at exactly the right time to destroy their enemy. A most terrible monster, the tiger explained, had come to live in the forest, and it was a creature like a gigantic spider, with a body as big as an elephant and legs as long as the trunks of trees. It crept through the forest and killed the animals, and no beast was able to resist it.

The Lion said that he would see to it, and he went away to look for the monster alone, leaving Dorothy and the others to wait. He found the creature asleep, and it looked so ugly that he almost turned away in disgust, but he remembered that the animals were relying on him. With one great leap and one mighty blow of his paw, he put an end to the monster, and he was surprised at how easy it had been.

When the Lion strode back to the clearing, the beasts bowed low before him, and the great tiger asked him to be their King and to protect them forever. The Lion said that he would be proud to do so, but that he must first see Dorothy safely home, and he promised to come back. Then the friends went on through the forest, and the Lion walked a little taller than before.

At last the forest ended in a steep, rocky hill, and the Scarecrow declared that they must climb it, since no other road lay in front of them. As they began to climb, a number of strange people with flat heads and short bodies came out from behind the rocks, and they shouted to the travelers to go back. They were called Hammer-Heads, and they had no arms, but their heads could shoot out upon long necks to strike any traveler.

When the Scarecrow tried to go forward, the head of one of the strange people shot out from his body on a long neck and knocked him down the hill, rolling over and over. Dorothy and the others ran back down to the bottom, and they agreed that it would be useless to fight such creatures. The Hammer-Heads laughed, and the Scarecrow suggested that Dorothy should call the Winged Monkeys.

Dorothy put on the Golden Cap and said the charm, and the Winged Monkeys appeared at once, as swift and eager as before. They lifted the friends in their strong arms and flew them high over the hill, and the Hammer-Heads, who could not reach them, stretched their necks and scowled up helplessly. The King of the Monkeys told Dorothy that this was her second command, and that she had one command left.

On the other side of the hill they came upon a beautiful land of red fences and red farmhouses and fields of red flowers, which was the country of the Quadlings. The people were plump, good-natured and dressed in red, and they gave the travelers a kindly welcome and told them where Glinda lived. They said that the Good Witch's castle was not far off, and that the road to it was easy to follow.

In front of the castle were three girls in handsome red uniforms trimmed with gold braid, and one of them asked why they had come to the South Country. Dorothy replied that they wished to see the Good Witch who ruled there, and she asked whether she could be taken to her at once. The girl asked for their names and went in to tell Glinda, while the travelers waited by the gate.

The travelers were led into a great hall where Glinda sat upon a throne of rubies, and they found her both beautiful and young. Her hair was a rich red and fell in ringlets over her shoulders, her dress was pure white, and her blue eyes looked kindly upon the little girl. She asked what she could do for Dorothy, and her voice was as sweet as music.

Dorothy told the Good Witch her whole story: how the cyclone had brought her to Oz, how she had found her companions, and what wonderful adventures they had met. She said that her greatest wish was to get back to Kansas, for Aunt Em would surely think something dreadful had happened to her. Unless the crops were better this year than last, she added, Uncle Henry could never afford the mourning clothes.

Glinda leaned forward and kissed the upturned face of the loving child, and said that she was sure she could tell her a way to get back to Kansas. But in return, she added, Dorothy must give her the Golden Cap, and Dorothy answered that she would do so willingly, since it was of no use to her now. Glinda smiled and said that she thought she would need the Winged Monkeys just three times.

Glinda turned to the Scarecrow and asked what he would do when Dorothy had left them, and he replied that he would return to the Emerald City, where Oz had made him ruler and the people liked him. His only worry, he said, was how to cross the hill of the Hammer-Heads. Glinda told him that she would command the Winged Monkeys to carry him to the gates of the city, since it would be a shame to deprive the people of so wonderful a ruler.

Then she asked the Tin Woodman what he would do, and he leaned on his axe for a moment before answering that the Winkies had been very kind to him and had wanted him to rule over them. He said that he would like nothing better, if only he could return to the Country of the West, than to rule over them forever and to be a good friend to them. The Witch promised that her second command to the Monkeys would be to carry him safely to the land of the Winkies, and she said that his brain might be smaller than the Scarecrow's but was brighter when well polished.

She asked the big shaggy Lion where he would go, and he answered that over the hill of the Hammer-Heads lay a grand old forest whose beasts had made him their King. Glinda promised him that her third command to the Monkeys would carry him safely to that forest, where he would pass his life very happily. Then, with the powers of the Golden Cap used up, she would give it to the King of the Monkeys, so that his band might be free for evermore.

The Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Lion thanked the Good Witch earnestly for her kindness, and Dorothy exclaimed that she was certainly as good as she was beautiful. But Glinda had not yet told her how to get back to Kansas, and the little girl, who could not forget this great need, asked her again. Glinda looked down at the girl's feet, and then she answered with a gentle smile that seemed to hold a secret which Dorothy could not yet understand.

“Your silver shoes will carry you over the desert,” said Glinda, “and if you had known their power you could have gone back to your Aunt Em the very first day you came to this country.” Dorothy stared at her feet in amazement, for she had worn the shoes ever since the Witch of the North gave them to her. All that time, the key to her wish had been shining on her own two feet.

“But then I should not have had my wonderful brains,” cried the Scarecrow, “for I might have passed my whole life in the farmer's cornfield.” The Tin Woodman added that he would never have had his lovely heart, and might have stood and rusted in the forest until the end of the world. The Lion declared that he would have lived a coward forever, and that no beast in all the forest would have had a good word to say for him.

Dorothy said that she was glad she had been of use to these good friends, and that now each of them had what he most desired, and a kingdom to rule besides, she should like to go back to Kansas. Glinda explained that the Silver Shoes had wonderful powers, and one of the most curious was that they could carry her to any place in the world in three steps, each made in the wink of an eye. All she had to do was to knock the heels together three times and command the shoes to take her wherever she wished.

Dorothy threw her arms around the Lion's great neck and kissed him, patting his big head as tenderly as she could. The Cowardly Lion, who had learned in these strange months what it was to be brave, sniffed and blinked back the tears that were shining in his eyes. He said that he would never forget how she had slapped his nose, and how she had made him feel like a king.

Then she kissed the Tin Woodman, who was weeping in a way most dangerous to his joints, so that she had to dry his face quickly with her apron. But she hugged the soft, stuffed body of the Scarecrow in her arms instead of kissing his painted face, and she found that she was crying herself at this sorrowful parting from her loving comrades. They had been so brave and clever, and they had made her journey so much less lonely.

Glinda the Good stepped down from her ruby throne to give the little girl a good-bye kiss, and Dorothy thanked her warmly for all the kindness she had shown to her friends and to herself. The Good Witch smiled, and in her sweet voice she wished the little traveler a safe and happy journey home. Around them, the guards in red and the girls of the castle stood in a quiet ring, as if they too were saying goodbye.

Dorothy took Toto up solemnly in her arms and, having said one last good-bye, clapped the heels of her silver shoes together three times. She gave her command very clearly, asking the shoes to take her home to Aunt Em, and for a moment nothing in the red hall moved. Her three dear friends and the lovely Witch watched her with their eyes full of love.

Instantly she was whirling through the air so swiftly that all she could see or feel was the wind whistling past her ears. The silver shoes took but three steps, each one as quick as the wink of an eye, and the whole green country of Oz melted away behind her. She held Toto close, with her eyes shut, and thought of nothing except the gray farm she loved.

The silver shoes took only three steps, and then she stopped so suddenly that she rolled over upon the grass several times before she knew where she was. At length she sat up and looked about her, and she cried “Good gracious” when she saw what lay before her eyes. She was sitting on the broad Kansas prairie, and the sky above her was the same wide sky she had known all her life.

Just before her stood the new farmhouse that Uncle Henry had built after the cyclone carried away the old one, small and plain and standing in the middle of the gray grass. It was not a grand house, and the paint was not yet burned off it by the sun, but to Dorothy's eyes it seemed the loveliest building in the world. She felt her heart begin to dance, and for a moment she could only stand and look at it with shining eyes.

Uncle Henry was milking the cows in the barnyard, with his gray head bent over the pail, and he had not yet seen her. Toto leaped out of her arms and ran barking furiously toward the barn, as if he wanted to tell the whole world that he was home again. Dorothy stood up and found that she was in her stocking feet, for the silver shoes had fallen off during her flight and were lost forever in the desert.

Aunt Em had just come out of the house to water the cabbages when she looked up and saw Dorothy running toward her across the grass. “My darling child,” she cried, folding the little girl in her arms and covering her face with kisses, and then she asked where in the world she had come from. She was crying and laughing at once, and she held Dorothy as though she would never let her go again.

“From the Land of Oz,” said Dorothy gravely, and she told her aunt that Toto had come back, too, and was safe. Then she hugged Aunt Em with all her strength, and she said, with a laugh and a sob, that she was so glad, so very glad, to be at home again. Gray as the prairie might be, it was her own, and there was no place in all the world that she loved so well.
